## Majjhima Nikāya
## Majjhima Paṇṇāsa Commentary
## Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-Awakened One
## 1. Gahapati Vagga
## 1. Explanation of the Kandaraka Sutta

The words beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" refer to the Kandaraka Sutta. In that sutta, "Campāyaṃ" means in the city named Campā. Indeed, in various places such as the parks and lotus ponds of that city, Champak (campaka) trees were abundant; therefore, it came to be known as Campā. "Gaggarāya pokkharaṇiyā tīre" means that not far from the city of Campā, there is a lotus pond called Gaggarā, so named because it was dug by the Chief Queen named Gaggarā. On the banks of that lotus pond, there is a large Champak forest adorned with flowers of five colors, such as blue. The Blessed One was staying in that Champak forest, which was fragrant with the scent of flowers. With reference to this, it is said, "Gaggarāya pokkharaṇiyā tīre."

"Mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ" means together with a large community of monks whose number is not specified (such as five hundred or three hundred). "Pesso" is the name of that person. "Hatthārohaputto" means the son of an elephant trainer. In the phrase "Kandarako ca paribbājako," Kandaraka is a wandering ascetic of that name who wears clothing.

"Abhivādetvā" means having paid homage to the Blessed One's feet, which are adorned with the marks of the wheel and possess the splendor of a blooming lotus the color of red lac. He did so as if entering into the midst of the dense six-colored Buddha-rays, as if being immersed in clear liquid lac, as if spreading out and wrapping himself, including his head, in a noble cloth the color of pure Siṅgī gold, as if receiving on his head Champak flowers endowed with color and fragrance, or as if he were the full moon approaching the foot of Mount Sineru. "Ekamantaṃ nisīdi" means he sat in a suitable place free from the six faults of sitting.
2:
He sat in a certain place, having paid homage to the feet which have the beauty of a blooming lotus.

"Tuṇှီbhūtaṃ tuṇှီbhūtaṃ" means that from whichever direction one looks, there is only silence. Among that assembly of monks, not even a single monk showed restlessness of hands or feet. All the monks, out of respect for the Blessed One and because of their own well-trained discipline, remained without conversing with one another. Without making even the slightest sound of clearing their throats, they sat surrounding the Blessed One like deeply planted gate-pillars, like the waters of the great ocean in a windless place, motionless in body and unscattered in mind, like crimson clouds surrounding the peak of Mount Sineru. Seeing the assembly of monks sitting thus in harmony, the wandering ascetic Kandaraka felt great joy and gladness (pīti-somanassa). Being unable to contain that arising joy and gladness within his heart, he spoke words of endearment. Therefore, he said the words beginning with "Acchariyaṃ bho."

In those words, something that does not happen constantly, like a blind man climbing to the top of a mountain, is called "acchariya" (wonderful). This is the linguistic method (saddanaya). According to the method of the Commentaries (aṭṭhakathānaya), it is called "acchariya" because it is worthy of snapping one's fingers. It means it is appropriate to snap one's fingers in appreciation. The occurrence of something that has never happened before is called "abbhuta" (extraordinary). Both of these are synonyms for wonder. That wonder is of two kinds: wonder by way of blame (garaha-acchariya) and wonder by way of praise (pasaṃsā-acchariya). Among these two, the words "Wonderful, Moggallāna! Extraordinary, Moggallāna! That this hollow man should wait even until his arm is grabbed" is called wonder by way of blame. The words "Wonderful, mother of Nanda! Extraordinary, mother of Nanda! In that you can even purify the arising of a thought" is called wonder by way of praise. Here, too, it is this wonder by way of praise that is intended. This is because the wandering ascetic spoke thus wishing to praise the Blessed One.

In the word "yāvañcidaṃ," "idaṃ" is merely a particle. "Yāva" is a word defining the extent. It means: to such an extent has [the Sangha] been well-trained that it is impossible to describe the virtues of that assembly of monks; rather, it is simply wonderful and extraordinary to have established them in such good practice to this extent. In the sentence "etaparamaṃyeva," the analysis is as follows: even for the assemblies of monks of past Buddhas, this assembly of monks, being so well-trained, is the ultimate limit; therefore, it is called "etaparama." It means that just as the Venerable Gotama has trained this assembly of monks, the past Buddhas also trained theirs in the same way; there is nothing beyond this. In the second method, it should be applied as: "Future Buddhas will also train them in this way; there is nothing beyond this." In that context, "paṭipādita" means being engaged in practice that is not contrary [to the Dhamma], beginning with the duties of proper conduct (ābhisamācārika-vatta). However, why does this wandering ascetic Kandaraka refer to the Buddhas of the past and future? Does he possess the knowledge of the three periods of time? He does not possess the knowledge of the three periods of time. Nevertheless, he speaks by way of adopting the method.
3:
The wanderer points to the Buddhas of the past and the future. Does this wanderer possess the knowledge that knows the three periods of time? He does not. However, standing on the basis of inference, he thinks: "This assembly of monks sits in such a manner; they are disciplined, trained, and peaceful. The Buddhas of the past also made just this much the pinnacle and caused [their followers] to practice. The Buddhas of the future will also cause [them] to practice. There is no practice superior to this." Thinking thus, he spoke with inferential knowledge (anubuddhi-ñāṇa).

"So it is, Kandaraka"—this statement is a separate connection (anusandhi) in the Pali text. It is said that the Blessed One, having heard those words, thought: "Kandaraka, you say that this assembly of monks is peaceful. However, the cause of this assembly's peace is not clear to you. You are not one who has fulfilled the thirty perfections (pāramīs), matured the roots of merit, and realized Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) at the seat of enlightenment (bodhi-pallaṅka). I, however, have fulfilled the perfections, brought to the pinnacle the conduct for the benefit of relatives (ñātattha-cariya), the conduct for the benefit of the world (lokattha-cariya), and the conduct for the benefit of Buddhahood (buddhattha-cariya), and realized Omniscience at the seat of enlightenment. To me, the cause of their peace is clear." To demonstrate this, He began this discourse.

"There are, Kandaraka..."—this statement is also a separate connection in the Pali text. It is said that this thought occurred to the Blessed One: "This wanderer says this assembly of monks is peaceful. This assembly of monks is not one that merely displays a peaceful appearance by composing their postures through deceit and hypocrisy while being mentally unpeaceful. In fact, in this assembly of monks, there are those who are still fulfilling the practice, and there are those who have finished the practice and reached the pinnacle. Among them, those who have finished the practice and reached the pinnacle are peaceful through the very virtues they have realized. Those still fulfilling the practice are peaceful through the insight (vipassanā) of the higher paths. Those remaining, apart from these, are peaceful through the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). I shall show him the cause of their peace." Thinking thus, He said, "There are, Kandaraka..." and so on, to show that "for this and that reason, this assembly of monks is peaceful."

Regarding the terms "Arahants, those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsavā)," etc., what should be said has already been stated in the commentary on the Mūlapariyāya Sutta. The practice of the trainees (sekha-paṭipada) was also detailed there. "Santatasīlā" means those of constant virtue, continuous virtue. "Santatavuttino" is a synonym for that same term; or it means those of constant livelihood. The meaning is that they lead their lives standing only in that constant virtue; they do not practice livelihood by breaking virtue, even if it means facing death.

"Nipakā" means the wise ones endowed with prudence (nepakka). "Nipakavuttino" means those who live by wisdom; they lead their lives standing in wisdom. Just as some in the Dispensation, having gone forth, for the sake of livelihood, frequent the six improper resorts (agocara)—frequenting prostitutes, widows, old maids, eunuchs, taverns, and nuns; or live in improper association with kings, royal ministers, sectarians, and their disciples; or practice medicine, act as messengers, run errands, lance boils, apply ointments, give emetics, give purgatives, prepare nasal oils, prepare medicinal oils, give bamboo, leaves, flowers, fruits, bathing powder, tooth-sticks, water for washing the face, or clay; or practice sycophancy, mung-bean-soup-like talk (flattery), acting as a menial, or running errands...
4:
Even after going forth in the Dispensation, for the sake of livelihood, one might frequent the six improper resorts. Prostitutes, widows, old maids, eunuchs, taverns, and nuns are improper resorts (agocara). One lives associating with kings, royal ministers, sectarians, and their disciples through improper social mixing. One practices medicine, acts as a messenger, runs errands, lances boils, applies ointments to wounds, gives emetics, gives purgatives, prepares nasal oils, prepares medicinal oils, gives bamboo, leaves, flowers, fruits, bathing powder, tooth-sticks, face-washing water, or clay. One practices sycophancy, mung-bean-soup-like talk (agreeable but false speech), acting as a menial, or running errands. A monk who leads his life through such twenty-one kinds of improper search (anesanā) is called one of unwise livelihood (anipakavutti). He does not lead his life standing in wisdom. After passing away from that life, he becomes a monk-demon (samaṇayakkha), and as it is said, "Even his outer robe is ablaze and glowing," he experiences great suffering.

One who is not of that kind, who does not transgress the training rules even for the sake of life, who stands in the fourfold purity of virtue (pārisuddhisīla), learns the Buddha's word to the best of one's ability, and fulfills the noble practices such as the Rathavinīta practice, Mahāgosiṅga practice, Mahāsuññata practice, Anaṅgaṇa practice, Dhammadāyāda practice, Nālaka practice, Tuvaṭṭaka practice, and Candopama practice—such ones become personal witnesses (kāyasakkhī) in the practice of the noble lineages (ariyavaṃsa), which involves contentment with the four requisites and delight in meditation. Like a bull elephant that has left the herd, like a lion free from the pack, or like a great ship without moorings, they dwell as solitary wanderers in their movements, etc., developing insight and exerting effort, thinking, "Today, even today, I shall attain Arahantship."

"Suppatiṭṭhitacittā" means having the mind well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). The remaining explanation of satipaṭṭhāna has been detailed below. Here, however, the foundations of mindfulness are spoken of as a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane. By this much, the cause of the assembly of monks' peace is explained.

"Yāva supaññattā" means well-established or well-expounded. By the words "We too, Bhante...", the wanderer Kandaraka intends to show that he himself is a practitioner and also intends to praise the assembly of monks. The meaning here is: "Bhante, although we are laypeople... we dwell with minds well-established [in mindfulness]. But for the assembly of monks, this establishment of the mind in mindfulness is like the plowing, the seed, the yoke and plow, the plowshare, and the goad. Therefore, the assembly of monks always has the foundations of mindfulness as their resort. We laypeople can only attend to these foundations of mindfulness when we have the opportunity. We too are those who attend to the foundations of mindfulness; we are not those who have entirely abandoned the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna)." "Manussagahane" refers to the entanglement caused by the messy desires of humans. It should be understood that those human desires are entangled due to the entanglement of defilements. In the terms "kasaṭasāṭheyya," it should be understood in the same way. Between those two, it is called "kasaṭa" in the sense of impurity, and "sāṭheyya" in the sense of deceit. "Sattānaṃ hitāhitaṃ jānāti" means thus...
5:
As for us humans, when we obtain the opportunity from time to time, we apply our minds to this mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhāna). We are also practitioners [of Satipaṭṭhāna]; we are not those whose meditation is entirely abandoned.

'Human thicket' (manussagahana) means the state of being entangled by the entanglement of human inclinations. It should be understood that their inclinations are also entangled by the entanglement of defilements (kilesa). The same method applies to the terms 'impurity' (kasaṭa) and 'deceit' (sāṭheyya). Among them, 'impurity' is understood by the sense of being unpurified, and 'deceit' is understood by the sense of being fraudulent. 'He knows the welfare and non-welfare of beings' means the Blessed One knows very well the practice that leads to the welfare and the practice that leads to the non-welfare of humans who are thus entangled, impure, and fraudulent.

In the phrase 'these animals' (yadidaṃ pasavo), 'animals' (pasavo) refers to all species of four-legged creatures. 'I am able' (pahomi) means I can. 'In such a short time' (yāvatakena antarena) means in such a moment. 'Will go to and from Campā' (campaṃ gatāgataṃ karissati) means they will go from the stable to the gate of the city of Campā and return. 'Deceits' (sāṭheyyāni) refers to acts of fraudulence. 'Crookedness' (kūṭeyyāni) refers to acts of trickery (like a crooked cow's tail). 'Bendings' (vaṅkeyyāni) refers to being bent (like a plow handle). 'Warpings' (jimheyyāni) refers to being warped (like the shape of a crescent moon). 'Will manifest' (pātukarissati) means will make clear or show. Indeed, that elephant or horse is unable to show those deceits and crookedness within such a short moment.

In that regard, for an elephant or horse that wishes to stand in a certain place, if that place is dangerous for humans, it does not have the thought, 'I will go forward and deceive them before standing.' It simply stands there with its four legs motionless like a fixed pillar. This is called 'deceit' (saṭha). Again, for one that wishes to throw off the person on its back, if that place is dangerous for humans, it does not think, 'I will go forward and deceive them before throwing him off.' It simply shakes [its body] and throws him off right there. This is called 'crookedness' (kūṭa). For one that wishes to turn back to the path it came from, if that place is dangerous for humans, it does not think, 'I will go forward and deceive them before doing so.' It simply leaves the path and returns to the previous path right there. This is called 'bending' (vaṅka). Again, for one that wishes to go sometimes to the left, sometimes to the right, or sometimes straight, if that place is dangerous for humans, it does not think, 'I will go forward and deceive them before doing so.' It simply goes left, right, or straight right there. Likewise, when it wishes to void excrement or urine, it does not think, 'This place is well-swept, crowded with people, and pleasant; it is not proper to void here, I will go forward and do it in a secluded place.' It simply voids right there. This is called 'warping' (jimha). Thus, this was said with reference to these four types of actions. All those...
6:
...deceits, crookedness, bendings, and warpings will be manifested; even while acting thus, those deceitful animals are said to manifest those deceits and so on.

Having thus shown the transparent nature of animals, now wishing to show the complex nature of humans, he said: 'But for us, Bhante, [our servants]...' and so on. In that passage, 'slaves' (dāsā) are those born in the house, bought with wealth, brought from war, or those who became slaves of their own accord. 'Messengers' (pessā) are those who carry out orders. 'Workers' (kammakarā) are those employed for food and wages. 'They act one way with the body' means they behave with the body in one manner, speak with words in another manner, and it shows that their mind is established in yet another manner.

Among them, some, seeing the master in his presence, go out to meet him, take the bundle from his hand, and setting aside what they have, take the master's things and perform all duties such as preparing the seat, fanning him, and washing his feet. But when he is behind their backs (in his absence), they do not even look at oil that is overflowing; even if work worth a hundred or a thousand is being ruined, they do not even wish to turn back and look. These are said to be those who act one way with the body. Some, in the presence of the master, praise him saying, 'Our master, our lord,' and so on. In his absence, there is no slander they will not say; they say whatever they wish. These are said to be those who act one way with speech.

'Pessa, these four types of persons...'—this is also a separate connection (anusandhi). In fact, this Pessa had said: 'Bhante, how wonderful it is that the Blessed One knows the welfare and non-welfare of beings while there is such human entanglement, such human impurity, and such human deceit.' The three persons mentioned previously follow a practice that is not for welfare; the fourth person to be mentioned hereafter follows a practice for welfare. Thus, the Buddha began this discourse to show, 'I know the welfare and non-welfare of beings.' It is also appropriate to connect this with the words of Kandaraka the wanderer mentioned below. Therefore, it is said: 'The Venerable Gotama has rightly guided the Saṅgha of monks.' Then, the Blessed One began this discourse also wishing to show: 'Having abandoned the three persons mentioned before, I guide them only in the practice for welfare of the fourth person mentioned hereafter.'

The word 'santo' is just a synonym for 'saṃvijjamānā' (existing). In the passage, 'They are peaceful (santā), calmed, and subsided,' those who have ceased are called 'santā'. In the passage, 'These dwellings are called peaceful (santā) in the discipline of the Noble One,' it refers to those whose defilements are extinguished. In the passage, 'The wise (santo) declare to the virtuous,' it refers to the wise. But here, it means existing or being found.
7:
In the words beginning with 'attantapa', one is called 'attantapa' because one torments or causes suffering to oneself. The practice of self-torment is called 'attaparitāpanānuyoga'. One is called 'parantapa' because one torments or causes suffering to others. The practice of tormenting others is called 'parapariṭāpanānuyoga'. 'Diṭṭhe va dhamme' means in this very existence (this selfhood). 'Nicchāta': Hunger is called 'chāta' (craving); since that person has no such craving, they are called 'nicchāta' (hungerless). Because all defilements have been extinguished, one is called 'nibbuta'. Because the defilements that cause internal heat no longer exist and one has reached coolness, one is called 'sītibhūta' (become cool). Because one experiences the happiness of jhāna, the path (magga), the fruit (phala), and nibbāna, one is called 'sukhapaṭisaṃvedī' (experiencing happiness). 'Brahmabhūtena attanā' means with a sublime self. 'Cittaṃ ārādheti' means to accomplish, fulfill, grasp, or purify the mind.

'Dukkhapaṭikkūlaṃ' means loathing suffering, not desiring suffering which is its opposite.

Regarding 'paṇḍita' (wise): Here, one is not called wise due to the four reasons, but one deserves to be called wise because of making an effort in the foundations of mindfulness (satippaṭṭhāna). Regarding 'mahāpañño' (one of great wisdom): This also should not be said based on the characteristics of a great wise person such as grasping great meanings, but one deserves to be called 'one of great wisdom' because of being endowed with the wisdom that grasps the foundations of mindfulness. 'Mahatā atthena saṃyutto agamiassā' means he would have gone endowed with the great benefit, which is the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala); it means he would have reached the fruit of stream-entry. Question: Can those who have the supporting condition (upanissaya) for the paths and fruits still face obstacles even when in the presence of the Buddhas? Yes, it can happen; however, it is not because of the Buddha, but rather due to the loss of action (kiriyaparihāni) or due to bad friendship (pāpamittatā). Among these, 'loss of action' means: If the General of the Dhamma (Venerable Sāriputta) had known the inclination of the Brahmin Dhanañjāni and preached the Dhamma accordingly, that Brahmin would have become a stream-enterer (sotāpanna). Thus, it happens due to the loss of action. 'Due to bad friendship' means: If King Ajātasattu had not listened to Devadatta's words and committed the act of parricide, he would have become a stream-enterer on the very day the Sāmaññaphala Sutta was preached. However, because he listened to his words and committed parricide, it did not happen. Thus, it happens due to bad friendship. For this lay follower Pessa, too, a loss of action occurred because he got up and left before the teaching was finished. 'Monks, even by this much, Pessa the elephant-driver's son is endowed with a great benefit.' With what great benefit is he endowed?
8: It is endowed with two benefits. That lay follower gained faith in the Saṅgha, and a new method for the practice of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) arose for him. Therefore, it is said, "associated with great benefit." Kandaraka the wanderer, however, only gained faith in the Saṅgha. "Etassa bhagavā kālo" means it is the time for this Dhamma teaching, or the time for classifying the four types of persons. In the words such as orabbhika, sheep are called urabbha, and one who kills sheep is an orabbhika. The same method applies to pig-butchers and so on. "Ludda" means one who is fierce and harsh. "Macchaghātaka" means a fisherman. "Bandhanāgārika" means a jailer. "Kururakammantā" means those who perform cruel deeds. "Muddhāvasitta" means a king anointed on the head with the royal consecration. "Puratthimena nagarassa" means on the eastern side of the city. "Santhāgāra" means a sacrificial hall. "Kharājinaṃ nivāsetvā" means having dressed in a rough antelope skin together with the hooves. "Sappiteleṇa" means with ghee and oil. Apart from ghee, any other oily substance is called tela (oil). "Kaṇḍူvamāno" means scratching with a horn at the time when scratching is needed because the fingernails have been cut. "Anantarahitāya" means on the bare ground without any spreading. "Sarūpavacchāya" means having a calf of the same color as the mother cow. If the cow is white, the calf is also white; if the cow is brindled or red, the calf is also like that; this is what is meant by sarūpavacchā. That anointed king says, "Kill the animals in this way." "Vacchatara" means young bulls that have passed the stage of being small calves and are strong. The same method applies to vacchatarī (heifers). "Barihisatthāya" means for the purpose of making a fence and for strewing on the sacrificial ground. The remaining words are clear in meaning as they have been explained in detail in the following suttas. ## The Commentary on the Kandaraka Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished. ## 2. Commentary on the Aṭṭhakanāgara Sutta "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so on is the Aṭṭhakanāgara Sutta. There, "Beluvagāmaka" means there is a small village named Beluva not far from the southern side of Vesālī; it means making that village a resort for alms. "Dasama" is so named because that householder is counted as the tenth in terms of birth and lineage, or in terms of the number of wealthy families.
9:
That householder is counted in the tenth place, both by lineage and by the count of his pleasing wealth. Therefore, the name 'Dasama' (Tenth) arose for that householder. 'Aṭṭhakanāgara' refers to the householder who resides in the city of Aṭṭhaka. 'Kukkuṭārāma' is the monastery built and offered by the merchant Kukkuṭa.

In the passage "Te na bhagavatā... akkhāto," the summary of the meaning is as follows: That Blessed One, having fulfilled the thirty perfections, destroyed all defilements, and realized the unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment. That Blessed One knows the inclinations and underlying tendencies (āsayānusaya) of various beings through his knowledge of inclinations and underlying tendencies. He sees all knowable things (ñeyyadhamma) through his unobstructed knowledge (anāvaraṇañāṇa), like a myrobalan fruit placed in the palm of his hand. Alternatively, he knows through knowledges such as the recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsa) and sees with the divine eye (dibbacakkhu). He knows through the three knowledges (vijjā) or the six higher powers (abhiññā) and sees with the 'Eye of All' (samantacakkhu), the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa), which is unobstructed in all things. He knows through the knowledge of omniscience, which is capable of knowing all phenomena, and sees with his extremely purified physical eye (maṃsacakkhu) even those forms located on the other side of a wall, which are beyond the range of the eyes of all ordinary beings. He knows through the wisdom of the Noble Path (ariyamagga), which has concentration as its basis and accomplishes his own benefit; and he sees through the wisdom of the Path of Teaching (desanāmagga), which has compassion as its root and accomplishes the benefit of others. He is called 'Arahaṃ' because he has destroyed the enemies of defilements and because he is worthy of receiving the four requisites. He is called 'Sammāsambuddha' because he has correctly and personally realized the Four Noble Truths. That Blessed One has thus taught. Alternatively, he is the one who knows the things that are obstacles to the Path and Fruition, sees the things that lead out of Saṃsāra, is called 'Arahaṃ' because he has abandoned the enemies of defilements, and is called 'Sammāsambuddha' because he has personally realized all phenomena. Thus, he is praised by these four reasons through the power of the Fourfold Knowledge of Fearlessness (catuvesārajjañāṇa). The summary meaning is: "Is there one Dhamma taught by the Blessed One?"

'Abhisaṅkhata' means a phenomenon that is made or produced. 'Abhisañcetayita' means a phenomenon that is intended or conditioned in various ways. 'So tattha ṭhito' means that the Non-returner who practices insight on that first jhāna remains established in that serenity and insight. By the two terms 'dhammarāgena dhammanandiyā,' the strong attachment (chandarāga) that occurs in serenity and insight is expressed. Indeed, one who is able to completely and utterly exhaust all attachment to serenity and insight becomes an Arahant; one who is unable to do so becomes a Non-returner. Because that Non-returner has not yet abandoned the attachment to serenity and insight, he is reborn in the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa) through the volition of the fourth jhāna. This is the unanimous explanation of the teachers.

However, a sophist (vitaṇḍavādī) says, "Because of the words 'by that very attachment to the Dhamma,' one is reborn in the Pure Abodes through unwholesome states." That person should be told, "Produce a Sutta passage for this." Being unable to find any other passage, he will surely produce this very passage. Then he should be asked, "Is this Sutta of the type whose meaning is to be inferred (neyyattha) or whose meaning is explicit (nītattha)?" He will certainly say it is of explicit meaning (nītattha). If that is the case...
10:
One who desires the fruit of Non-returning would then have to cultivate attachment to serenity and insight; and if attachment is produced, the fruit of Non-returning would be realized. Saying "I have found the Sutta," he presents various Pali passages to prove his view. One who wishes to answer a problem should learn from a teacher and realize the essence of the meaning before teaching. There is no such thing as rebirth in a heavenly realm due to unwholesome kamma, or rebirth in a woeful state due to wholesome kamma.

The Blessed One taught this— "Monks, by kamma born of greed, kamma born of hatred, and kamma born of delusion, gods are not known, humans are not known, nor are any other happy realms known. On the contrary, monks, it is only by kamma born of greed, hatred, and delusion that hell, the animal realm, the peta realm, and other woeful states are known." Thus should he be made to understand. If he understands, let him understand; if he does not, he should be dismissed by saying, "Go to the monastery early and drink your congee."

Just as in this Sutta, serenity and insight are also taught in the Mahāmālukyovāda Sutta, the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta, and the Kāyagatāsati Sutta. Among these, in this Sutta, whether one proceeds by the way of serenity or by the way of insight, serenity alone is the lead (dhura). In the Mahāmālukyovāda Sutta, insight alone is the lead. The Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta is taught as insight-dominant (vipassanuttara), and the Kāyagatāsati Sutta is taught as serenity-dominant (samathuttara).

"Ayaṃ kho gahapati... ekadhammo akkhāto" means that when asked about a single Dhamma, it is answered as "this too is a single Dhamma" by the power of the question; thus all eleven Dhammas come to be called 'Single Dhamma' (ekadhamma). Just as in the Mahāsakuludāyī Sutta, nineteen sections are called 'Single Dhamma' by the power of the path of practice, here they appear as 'Single Dhamma' because of the eleven questions. Alternatively, because they all have the same benefit of reaching the Deathless (amata), it is appropriate to call them all 'Single Dhamma'.

'Nidhimukhaṃ gavesanto' refers to a person searching for a treasure pot. 'Sakideva' means with a single effort. How can one obtain eleven treasure pots with just a single effort? In this world, a certain person wanders in the forest searching for a treasure pot. A well-wisher sees him and asks, "Friend, why are you wandering?" He replies, "Wealth, which is the means of livelihood..."
11:
“I am searching,” he said. The other said, “Friend, if so, come; roll this stone slab.” He rolled the stone and saw eleven pots of gold, either placed one upon another or touching belly to belly. Thus, with a single effort, eleven treasures were obtained.

“We will seek wealth for the teacher”: Outside the Dispensation, sectarians (titthiyas) give wealth to the teacher from whom they learn an art, either before, after, or during the course of learning, by taking it from their homes. If there is no wealth in the disciples' homes, they seek it from relatives. If they still cannot find it, they even go on alms-round to give it. This is said in reference to that.

“Why should I not do so?”: Even those outside the Dispensation seek wealth for a teacher who merely gives secular knowledge in a teaching that does not lead to liberation. Why then should I not pay homage to the teacher, the Venerable Ānanda, who teaches the elevenfold practice for attaining the Deathless in such a Dispensation that leads to liberation? I will certainly do so.

“He clothed each monk with a pair of cloths”: This means he gave a pair of cloths to each individual monk. The word “acchādesi” (clothed) is used here as a common worldly expression. “A monastery worth five hundred”: This means he had a leaf-roofed hut built worth five hundred (units of currency). The rest of the words are clear everywhere.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Aṭṭhakanāgara Sutta is finished.
## 3. Explanation of the Sekha Sutta

“Evaṃ me sutaṃ” and so forth is the Sekha Sutta. In that sutta, “a new Santhāgāra” means a large hall (assembly hall) that has just been built. When going out to war, kings stand there and make arrangements (santham), setting boundaries: “Let this many troops go in front, this many behind, this many on both sides; let this many mount elephants, this many horses, and this many stay in chariots.” Therefore, that place is called “Santhāgāra.” Also, after returning from the place of mobilization, while they are cleaning their houses with fresh cow-dung and so on, the kings rest (santhambhanti) there for two or three days; thus it is called Santhāgāra. It is also called Santhāgāra because it is the hall (agāra) where those kings govern (anusāsana) together. For the kings of a republic...
12:
...those kings who govern for the common good assemble. Therefore, a matter that has arisen cannot be decided by the will of a single person; it is proper to obtain the consent of all. Thus, all the kings assemble there and give counsel. Therefore, I, the commentator, say “Santhāgāra” in the sense of “a hall for governing together for the common good.” Alternatively, those kings assemble in that great hall and deliberate on various household matters, such as “At this time it is proper to plow, at this time it is proper to sow.” Thus, because they arrange (santharanti) the various affairs of household life there, it is called Santhāgāra.

“It was recently built” (acirakāritaṃ hoti): It is a building just completed, like a celestial mansion, well-decorated with woodwork, stonework, and painting.

“By a recluse or...” (samaṇena vā): The meaning should be understood here. Because deities take possession of their dwelling places only at the time of acquiring the house-site, it was not said “by a god,” but “by a recluse, or a brahmin, or any human being.”

“They approached the Blessed One”: Having heard that the assembly hall was finished, they thought, “Let us go and see that hall.” They went and inspected the entire building starting from the gateway. They thought, “This assembly hall is extremely delightful and magnificent, like a celestial mansion. Who should use it first so that it may be for our long-term welfare and happiness?” Then they decided, “Even if it were first given to our noble kinsmen, it is only fitting for the Teacher; even if given by way of being a worthy recipient of offerings, it is only fitting for the Teacher. Therefore, let us first have the Teacher use it. We will invite the Saṅgha of monks. When the Saṅgha of monks arrives, the Word of the Buddha known as the Tipiṭaka will also arrive. We will have the Teacher deliver a Dhamma talk to us throughout the three watches of the night. Thus, after the hall has been used by the Three Jewels, we will use it later. Doing so will be for our long-term welfare and happiness.” Having made this resolution, they approached the Blessed One.

“They approached the assembly hall”: It is said that on that day, although the assembly hall was well-prepared and decorated like a celestial mansion for the inspection of the royal families, it had not yet been laid out in a manner suitable for the Buddha. For Buddhas, by nature, incline toward the forest and delight in the forest; they may or may not stay inside a village. Therefore, thinking, “We will lay it out only after knowing the Blessed One’s mind,” those Sakyans approached the Blessed One. Now, having obtained his consent and wishing to lay it out, they approached the place where the assembly hall was.

“Having spread the entire assembly hall” (sabbasanthariṃ santhāgāraṃ santharitvā): This means having it prepared so that everything is completely spread. First of all, thinking “Cow-dung is auspicious for all blessings,” they had the floor, even though made of plaster, cleansed with liquid cow-dung. When they knew the surroundings were dry, they had it smeared so that no footprints would appear when stepped upon...
13:
Thinking, 'It is suitable,' they had the ground, which was already well-prepared with plaster, wiped with moist cow dung. Knowing it was dry all around so that no footprints would appear where stepped upon, they had it smeared with the four types of perfumes and had mats of various colors spread above. On top of those mats, starting with large carpets used on elephants' backs, they had the entire area covered with various colored rugs such as those with patterns of elephants, horses, lions, tigers, the moon, the sun, and intricate floral designs. Regarding this, it is said: 'Having spread the assembly hall with all kinds of floor coverings.'

'Having prepared the seats' means: Having prepared the Blessed One's highly valuable seat near the auspicious central pillar in the middle, and having spread soft and delightful coverings on that seat, they placed a beautiful red cushion for the Blessed One. Above it, they hung a canopy adorned with gold and silver stars, decorated it with garlands of perfumes, flowers, and leaves. They made a floral net covering twelve cubits around, enclosed an area of about thirty cubits with curtains, and near the western wall, they prepared various types of couches and benches—with backrests and without—for the Saṅgha of monks, covering them with white cloths. Near the eastern wall, they spread large carpets for themselves and placed pillows filled with swan down and other materials, thinking, 'In this way, we shall listen to the Dhamma all night without fatigue.' Regarding this preparation, it is said: 'Having prepared the seats.'

'A large water jar' refers to a wide-bellied water vessel. 'Having placed it nearby' means: So that the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks could wash their hands, feet, or faces as they pleased, they filled jars in various places with water clear as jewels. To make it fragrant, they added various flowers and scented powders, covered them with banana leaves, and set them in place. Regarding this, it is said: 'Having placed it nearby.'

'Having lit the oil lamps' means: Lighting oil lamps in torches made of silver, gold, etc., and in lamps held in the hands of statues of Yonakas, Kirātas, and others. 'They approached where the Blessed One was': In this context, those Sakyan kings did not only decorate the assembly hall; they also had the streets of the city of Kapilavatthu, which was one league in circumference, swept and cleaned...
14:
They had banners and flags hoisted, placed full jars and banana trees at the doors of houses, and made the entire city look as if it were strewn with stars by means of rows of lamps. They had the drum beaten, announcing: 'Let the nursing infants be fed; feed the young children early and put them to sleep; do not make loud noises. Tonight, the Teacher will stay within the village for the whole night. Those known as Buddhas desire quietness.' Then, carrying torches themselves, they approached where the Blessed One was.

Then the Blessed One, having dressed and taking his bowl and robes, went to the new assembly hall together with the Saṅgha of monks. When it was announced that it was time, saying, 'Venerable Sir, it is now time for the Blessed One to depart,' the Blessed One adjusted his double under-robe, which was dyed with lac and had the color of a moist, red Kovilāra flower, as neatly as if cutting a lotus with scissors, and dressed so as to cover the three circles. He fastened his waistband, which was as glorious as a flash of lightning, as if encircling a bunch of lotuses with a golden cord. He donned his noble rag-robe (paṃsukūla), which had the color of a young banyan leaf, which he himself had taken after shaking the great earth along with the Cakkavāḷa, Mount Sineru, and Mount Yugandhara. He appeared like a lion coming out of a golden cave, or like the full moon rising from the peak of Mount Udaya, as he emerged from the door of the Perfumed Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), looking as if a red blanket were draped over an elephant's frontal globes, or as if a coral net were cast over a golden pagoda a hundred cubits high, or as if a golden stupa were covered with a red woolen mantle, or as if the moving full moon were obscured by a red cloud, or as if refined lac-dye were poured over the peak of a golden mountain, or as if the peak of Mount Cittakūṭa were encircled by lightning. After emerging, he stood in front of the Perfumed Chamber.

As he stood there, rays of light issued from his body like flashes of lightning from the clouds, making the trees in the monastery appear as if they were trees filled with sprouts, leaves, flowers, and fruits showered with liquid gold. At that very moment, the great Saṅgha of monks, taking their own bowls and robes, surrounded the Blessed One.

The monks standing in attendance were of such nature: having few desires, contented, secluded, not associating with crowds, energetic, skillful in speech, patient, self-admonishing, censuring evil, and endowed with virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. Surrounded by those monks, the Blessed One shone like a golden mass surrounded by red blankets, like a golden boat in the middle of a red lotus thicket, or like a golden palace surrounded by coral railings. The great elders, such as Sāriputta and Moggallāna, also [attended] the Blessed One, who had the color of a dark rain cloud...
15:
The great elders, led by the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, wearing dust-heap robes (paṃsukūla) the color of dark rain clouds, surrounded the Blessed One like great noble elephants adorned with jeweled armor. These elders were free from lust, had destroyed the defilements, were free from entanglements, and had severed all bonds; they were unattached to family or group. Thus, the Blessed One, being himself free from lust, was surrounded by Arahants who were free from lust; being himself free from hatred, he was surrounded by Arahants who were free from hatred; being himself free from delusion, he was surrounded by Arahants who were free from delusion; being himself free from craving, he was surrounded by Arahants who were free from craving; being himself free from defilements, he was surrounded by Arahants who were free from defilements; and being himself the Awakened One who realized the Four Noble Truths, he was surrounded by Arahants of great learning.

He set out on the journey to the city of Kapilavatthu with incomparable Buddha-appearance and immeasurable Buddha-splendor, like a lotus filament surrounded by petals, like a lotus pericarp surrounded by filaments, like the Chaddanta elephant king surrounded by eight thousand elephants, like the Dhataraṭṭha swan king surrounded by ninety thousand swans, like a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) surrounded by his fourfold army, like Sakka, King of Devas, surrounded by the host of gods, like Hārita Mahābrahmā surrounded by the host of Brahmās, and like the full moon surrounded by the host of stars.

As he proceeded, golden rays emerged from the front of the Blessed One's body and spread to a distance of eighty cubits. Golden rays also emerged from the back of his body, from his right shoulder, and from his left shoulder, spreading to a distance of eighty cubits. From the tips of his hair upwards, rays the color of a peacock's neck emerged from every curl and spread eighty cubits into the sky. From the soles of his feet downwards, coral-colored rays emerged and spread eighty cubits into the solid earth. Thus, in every direction for eighty cubits, the six-colored Buddha-rays (chabbaṇṇaraṃsi) shone and vibrated, darting forth like golden lamps, like flames leaping into the sky, or like streaks of lightning flashing from a great cloud that covers the four great islands.

All directions appeared as if strewn with golden champak flowers, as if poured with streams of liquid gold from golden jars, as if draped with outspread golden cloth, or as if covered with the powder of kiṃsuka and kaṇikāra flowers stirred up by the Veramba winds. The Blessed One's body, radiant with the eighty minor marks (anubyañjana), the fathom-wide radiance (byāmappabhā), and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (mahāpurisalakkhaṇa), was as beautiful as the starry sky, as a blooming lotus pond, or as a Pāricchattaka tree a hundred yojanas in size in full bloom from root to tip. He shone, surpassing the glory of thirty-two moons, the glory of thirty-two suns, the glory of thirty-two Universal Monarchs, and the glory of thirty-two kings of devas...
16:
(The Blessed One) shone as if surpassing the glory of thirty-two Great Brahmās. This splendor was due to his being adorned with the thirty perfections: the ten perfections (pāramī), the ten higher perfections (upapāramī), and the ten ultimate perfections (paramatthapāramī), all fully perfected. The acts of giving, the virtue observed, and the meritorious deeds performed over a period of four incalculable eons (asaṅkheyya) and a hundred thousand eons (kappa) seemed to be crowded together, seeking an opportunity to bear fruit within a single existence. It was like loading the cargo of a thousand ships into a single ship, or the cargo of a thousand carts into a single cart, or like the currents of twenty-five rivers converging at a single river mouth.

Even though he was shining with such Buddha-glory, thousands of torches were carried in front of the Blessed One. Likewise, torches were carried behind him, and on his left and right sides. Flowers such as jasmine, great jasmine, forest jasmine, red lotus, blue lotus, and sinduvāra, as well as fragrant powders of blue, yellow, and other colors, fell scattered like rain from a cloud covering the four great islands. The sounds of the fivefold musical instruments and the voices of praise concerning the virtues of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha filled all directions. The eyes of devas, humans, nāgas, supaṇṇas, gandhabbas, yakkhas, and others felt as if they were receiving a drink of ambrosia (amata). At this point, it is fitting to describe the manner of his journey with a thousand verses. Of that praise, this is but a brief summary:

Endowed thus with all auspicious attributes,
Shaking the earth as he goes,
Without harming any living beings,
The Leader of the World proceeds.

Lifting the right foot first,
The Bull among Men, full of glory,
The Best of Bipeds shines
As he goes.

As the Most Excellent Buddha walks,
His soft soles touch the ground evenly,
Yet he is not defiled
By any dust.

When the Leader of the World walks,
Low places rise up,
And high places become level;
Even the inanimate earth (responds).

Stones, pebbles, potsherds,
Stumps, and thorns—
All clear away from the path
When the Leader of the World walks.
17: He does not lift his foot too far, nor does he set it down too near. He walks without his knees or ankles knocking against each other. The Sage, possessed of perfect conduct, does not walk too quickly, nor does he walk too slowly; he walks composed and concentrated. That Blessed One does not look upwards, downwards, or sideways, nor towards the cardinal or intermediate directions; he walks looking only a yoke's length ahead. With the gait of a noble elephant, the Victorious One appears beautiful in his walking. The Supreme One of the world walks gracefully, gladdening the world of devas and humans. Shining like the moon, like a maned lion, delighting many beings, he arrived at the noble city of Kapilavatthu. This time is called the "time for praise" (vaṇṇakāla). At such a time, in praising the physical beauty or the qualities of the Buddha, the capability of the Dhamma speaker is the only measure. One should praise as much as possible, whether through prose passages (cuṇṇiya) or through the composition of verses (gāthā). It should not be said that it is poorly spoken. For the Buddhas possess immeasurable qualities. Even the Buddhas themselves are unable to fully describe those qualities without remainder, let alone other beings. Having entered the city of the Sakyan kings, which was decorated and prepared with such splendor, the Blessed One, being worshiped with scents, incense, and aromatic powders by the people with confident hearts, entered the Santhāgāra hall. With reference to that, it was said: "Then the Blessed One, having dressed and taking his bowl and robe, approached the Santhāgāra hall together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus." "With the Blessed One alone at the head" means placing the Blessed One in front. There, the Blessed One, while sitting in the midst of the bhikkhus and the lay followers, having been bathed with scented water, having the water wiped away with a cloth, and being rubbed with pure vermilion, shone exceedingly like a solid red-gold statue placed on a seat draped with a red rug. This is the method of praising qualities by the ancient teachers: "Having gone to the circular hall (maṇḍalamāḷa), with the gait of a noble elephant, illuminating with the six-colored rays, the Supreme One of the world sat down on the noble seat."
18:
Sitting there, the Charioteer of men to be tamed,
The God above gods, endowed with the marks of a hundred merits,
The Buddha shines in the midst of the assembly,
Like a pure gold Nikkha placed upon a crimson rug.

Like a Nikkha of Jambūnada gold placed on a crimson rug,
Like a radiant gem free from impurities,
The Blessed One, free from all stains, shines brilliantly.

Like a great Sal tree in full bloom,
Like the adorned King of Mountains (Meru),
Like a polished golden pillar,
Like the red lotus known as Kokanada,

Like a flaming lamp-tree,
Like a fire burning on a mountain top,
Like the Parichattaka tree of the gods in full bloom,
So did He shine.

In the phrase 'kāpilavatthave sakye bahudeva rattiṃ dhammiyā kathāyā', 'Dhamma talk' (dhammī kathā) should be understood as a miscellaneous discourse connected with the appreciation (anumodanā) of the assembly hall. At that time, the Blessed One delivered a miscellaneous Dhamma talk that brought welfare and happiness to the Sakyans living in Kapilavatthu, as if letting down the celestial Ganges, as if drawing out the essence of the earth, as if shaking the branches of a great Jambu tree, or as if making them drink honey by squeezing a league-wide honeycomb with a machine. He spoke many Dhamma discourses, varied in many ways, saying: "Great King, this gift of a dwelling is of great benefit. This hall of yours has been used by Me, it has been used by the Saṅgha of monks; having been used by Me and the Saṅgha, it is indeed used by the Jewel of the Dhamma. Thus, it is said to be used by the Triple Gem. When the gift of a dwelling (āvāsadāna) is given, all gifts are considered given. The merit of a leaf-hut built on the ground or a pavilion of branches cannot be measured." Having spoken thus, He said:

"A monastery wards off cold and heat,
And also wild beasts,
Reptiles, mosquitoes,
The cold season, and the rains.

Furthermore, it wards off the fierce wind and sun
When they arise.
For the sake of shelter and comfort,
And for the sake of meditation and insight,

The gift of a monastery to the Saṅgha
Is praised by the Buddha as the highest.
Therefore, a wise man,
Seeing his own benefit..."
19:
One should have delightful monasteries built and settle the learned there. To those learned ones, one should offer food, drink, clothing, and lodgings. One should give with a clear mind to those of upright disposition. They will preach the Dhamma that dispels all suffering to that donor. Having understood that Dhamma in this Dispensation, one becomes free from taints and attains Nibbāna.

Thus, this benefit is also the benefit obtained from a monastery; this benefit is also the benefit obtained from a monastery—thus, for much of the night, exceeding one and a half watches, he preached the Dhamma talk concerning the benefits of monasteries. Among those talks on benefits, only these verses were included in the Council; the miscellaneous Dhamma teachings, however, were not included. The words beginning with 'sandassesi' have the meanings already explained.

The phrase 'He addressed the Venerable Ānanda' means he informed him because he wished him to deliver a Dhamma talk. Why did the Blessed One place the burden of preaching on the Elder Ānanda while the eighty great elders such as the Venerable Sāriputta, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, and the Venerable Mahākassapa were present? It was due to the disposition of the assembly. The Venerable Ānanda is the foremost among the learned and is well-known among the Sakyan clan for his ability to deliver sweet Dhamma talks with well-rounded phrases and syllables. Although the Sakyan kings had heard the Venerable Ānanda’s Dhamma talks by going to the monastery, the women of their inner court could not go to the monastery as they pleased. It occurred to those Sakyan kings: 'Oh, if only the Blessed One would preach just a little Dhamma and then entrust the task of preaching to our noble kinsman Ānanda!' Knowing their disposition, the Blessed One entrusted the task of preaching to the Venerable Ānanda alone.

'Sekho pāṭipado' refers to a trainee monk (sekha) endowed with the practice. 'Let that practice of the trainee be clear to you; preach the practice to him'—thus he points out the person by specifying the practice. Why did the Blessed One specify this practice? There are many reasons. Firstly, these Sakyans desire a blessing (maṅgala) and prosperity in the auspicious hall. This practice of a trainee is also the auspicious practice and the practice of growth in my Dispensation; therefore, he specified this practice. Furthermore, many trainees were sitting in that assembly; he specified this practice considering that they would be able to note it without fatigue if what they themselves had penetrated was preached. Also, the Venerable Ānanda has attained the analytical knowledge (paṭisambhidā) of a trainee; he specified this practice considering that Ānanda would be able to make them understand without fatigue while preaching what he himself had personally penetrated. In the practice of a trainee, the three trainings are also...
20:
...included. Among those three trainings, when the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) is preached, the entire Vinaya Piṭaka is considered preached. When the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā) is preached, the entire Suttanta Piṭaka is considered preached. When the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā) is preached, the entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka is considered preached. The Venerable Ānanda is learned and a bearer of the Tipiṭaka. He is capable of preaching the three trainings by means of the three Piṭakas. Considering that if preached in this way, it would lead only to the blessing and prosperity of the Sakyans, he specified this practice of a trainee.

Why did he say, 'My back aches'? While the Blessed One was striving in his great exertion (padhāna) for six years, great bodily suffering occurred. Later, in his old age, wind-ailment (piṭṭhivāta) arose in his back. Or else, this statement is not without reason. The Blessed One is capable of suppressing the arisen feeling and sitting in a single cross-legged posture for one day, two days, or even seven days. However, he wished to make use of the assembly hall (santhāgāra) with the four postures. In that hall, by walking from the place of washing the feet to the Dhamma seat, the posture of walking was accomplished. Having reached the Dhamma seat and standing for a moment, the posture of standing was accomplished. By sitting on the Dhamma seat for one and a half watches, the posture of sitting was accomplished. He thought, 'Now, by reclining for a while on the right side, the posture of lying down will be accomplished.' Thus, he wished to make use of it with the four postures. It cannot be said that the 'clung-to body' (upādinnaka-sarīra) does not ache. Therefore, he spoke thus, taking as a reason the slight ache produced by sitting for a long time.

'Having had the outer robe (saṅghāṭi) spread' means: it is said that on one side of the assembly hall, those kings had a curtained enclosure made, a suitable couch prepared, and covered with suitable rugs. Above it, they hung a canopy adorned with golden stars, scented garlands, and flower tassels, and lit scented oil lamps. They prepared it thinking, 'Perhaps the Teacher, having risen from the Dhamma seat and resting for a while, might recline here. If the Blessed One makes use of this assembly hall with the four postures in this way, it will be for our long-term welfare and happiness.' The Teacher also, intending that very wish of the Sakyans, had his outer robe spread there and reclined. 'Mindful of the time to rise' means: placing in his mind the perception of rising, thinking, 'I shall rise after this much time has passed.'

'He addressed Mahānāma the Sakyan' means: it is said that at that time, Mahānāma was the chief and leader in that assembly. Considering that if Mahānāma was included, the rest of the assembly would also be included, the Venerable Ānanda addressed and spoke only to Mahānāma.
21:
The Elder Ānanda thought that if he could win over Mahānāma the Sakyan, the rest of the assembly would also be won over. Thus, he addressed Mahānāma specifically. 'Sīlasampanno' means endowed with virtue, possessing perfect virtue, or having complete virtue. 'Saddhammehi' means with good qualities or with the teachings of the virtuous (sappurisa).

With the phrase 'Kathañca Mahānāma,' he set out the outline (mātikā) of the trainee’s practice (sekha-paṭipadā) and spoke thus because he wished to elaborate on it in sequence. In that context, 'sīlasampanno' and so forth should be understood according to the method taught in the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta, etc., which says, 'Monks, dwell endowed with virtue.'

In the terms 'kāya-duccaritena' and so forth, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the accusative. It means being ashamed of and loathing bodily misconduct and so on. In the explanation of 'ottappa' (moral dread), the instrumental case is used in the sense of cause. It means being afraid or fearful because of bodily misconduct, etc., which are the causes of moral dread. 'Āraddha-vīriyo' means having aroused energy and an undaunted mind. 'Pahānāya' means for the sake of abandoning. 'Upasampadāya' means for the sake of attaining. 'Thāmavā' means endowed with the strength of energy. 'Daḷha-parakkamo' means having firm effort. 'Anikkhitta-dhuro kusalesu dhammesu' means not laying down the burden regarding wholesome states, having unflagging energy. 'Paramena' means supreme. 'Sati-nepakkena' means endowed with mindfulness and keen wisdom. Why is wisdom included in the analysis of mindfulness? To show the great power of mindfulness. For mindfulness dissociated from wisdom is weak, while mindfulness associated with wisdom is powerful.

'Cirakatampi' refers to the fulfillment of the eighty great duties, such as the duties of the shrine courtyard, performed long ago by oneself or others with the body. 'Cirabhāsitampi' refers to verbal action (vaci-kamma) performed long ago by oneself or others through speech, such as respectful learning, teaching, reciting, preaching the Dhamma, discussing the Dhamma, and giving thanks (anumodanā). 'Saritā anussaritā' means that regarding what was done long ago with the body, one thinks: 'The body is bodily intimation (kāya-viññatti); in what was spoken long ago, the speech is vocal intimation (vaci-viññatti). Both are form (rūpa). The consciousness and mental factors that originate them are non-form (nāma). Thus, these phenomena of form and non-form, having arisen in this way, ceased in this way.' By thus remembering and repeatedly recollecting, one arouses the mindfulness enlightenment factor (sati-sambojjhaṅga). This is the meaning. For here, the mindfulness that arouses the enlightenment factor is intended. Through that mindfulness, this person is called 'saritā' due to remembering even once, and 'anussaritā' due to remembering repeatedly.
22:
'Udayatthagāminiyā' refers to wisdom that goes towards arising and passing away, capable of penetrating the arising and passing away of the five aggregates. 'Ariyāya' means pure wisdom that stands far from defilements through abandoning by suppression (vikkhambhana) and abandoning by eradication (samuccheda). 'Paññāya samannāgato' means being endowed with both insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) and path wisdom (magga-paññā). 'Nibbedhikāya' is so called because that very wisdom penetrates; it means one who is endowed with that wisdom. Therein, path wisdom is 'nibbedhikā' because, through abandoning by eradication, it penetrates and breaks through the mass of greed, the mass of hatred, and the mass of delusion, which were never penetrated or broken through before. Insight wisdom also deserves to be called 'nibbedhikā' because it penetrates the mass of defilements through abandoning by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna), and because it leads to the attainment of the penetrative path wisdom. In the phrase 'sammā dukkha-kkhaya-gāminiyā,' path wisdom is called 'sammā dukkha-kkhaya-gāminī' because it proceeds by exhausting the suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha) through the right causal method. Insight wisdom is 'dukkha-kkhaya-gāminī' because it proceeds by exhausting the suffering of the round and the suffering of defilements through abandoning by substitution of opposites. Alternatively, this insight should be known as 'dukkha-kkhaya-gāminī' because it brings about the attainment of path wisdom, which is the end of suffering.

'Abhicetasikānaṃ' refers to the jhānas that depend on the higher mind (the noble mind). 'Diṭṭhadhamma-sukha-vihārānaṃ' refers to the jhānas that are the cause for obtaining happiness in every moment of attainment. 'Nikāmalābhī' is one who can enter [the jhānas] at any desired moment. 'Akicchalābhī' is one who obtains them without difficulty. 'Akasiralābhī' is one who obtains them abundantly. Some practitioners can enter at any desired moment but cannot remove the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), which are obstacles to concentration, without difficulty; thus, they may emerge from the jhāna quickly against their will and cannot maintain the attainment for the determined duration. Such a person is called 'kicchalābhī' (obtaining with difficulty) and 'kasiralābhī' (obtaining with trouble). Another person can enter at any desired moment and also remove the hindrances without difficulty; he can emerge from the jhāna exactly according to the determined duration. Such a person is called 'akicchalābhī' and 'akasiralābhī'.

'Ayaṃ vuccati mahānāma ariyasāvako sekho pāṭipado' means: 'Mahānāma, this noble disciple is called a trainee (sekha) who is endowed with the practice that grows with the womb of insight.' 'Apuccaṇḍatāya' is because of having insight wisdom like an unrotten egg. 'Bhabbo abhinibbhidāya' means being capable of breaking through with insight and knowledges such as the recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa). 'Sambodhāya' means for the sake of the Noble Path. 'Anuttarassa yogakkhemassa' means...
23:
It shows that he is fit to attain the Fruit of Arahantship, which is called the unsurpassed security from bondage (yogakkhema). The simile brought here in this Sekha Sutta to clarify the meaning should be understood in the same way as stated in the Cetokhila Sutta. Indeed, in that Cetokhila Sutta, the comparison is given as: "Just as that hen performs three kinds of actions upon the eggs, so too should the state of this monk being endowed with the fifteen factors of exertion be understood." In this Sekha Sutta, however, it should be understood by applying it thus: "The endowment with the fifteen qualities such as perfection in virtue is like that hen performing three kinds of actions upon the eggs." The remaining words are just as stated in all other places.

"This unsurpassed purity of mindfulness due to equanimity" refers to the purity of mindfulness arising from equanimity associated with the noble fourth jhāna, which is unlike the first jhāna and so on. "First breaking out" (paṭhama-abhinibbhidā) means the first piercing through of knowledge. The same method applies to the second and subsequent breakings out. A young chick is born twice: once from the mother's womb and once from the eggshell. The noble disciple is born three times through the three true knowledges (vijjā). Having dispelled the darkness (delusion) that covers past lives, he is born for the first time through the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa). Having dispelled the darkness that covers the passing away and rebirth of beings, he is born for the second time through the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa). Having dispelled the darkness that covers the Four Noble Truths, he is born for the third time through the knowledge of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa).

"This also belongs to this monk's conduct (caraṇa)" means that this virtue also constitutes the conduct of that monk. Conduct is manifold and of various kinds, consisting of fifteen qualities such as virtue; here, it means this virtue is one part of that conduct. As for the meaning of the word, it is called 'conduct' (caraṇa) because by means of it, one goes to a destination never reached before. This method applies to all terms.

"This also belongs to this monk's true knowledge (vijjā)" means that this knowledge of recollecting past lives constitutes the true knowledge of that monk. True knowledge is manifold and of various kinds, consisting of eight knowledges such as insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa); here, it means this knowledge is one part of that true knowledge. As for the meaning of the word, it is called 'true knowledge' (vijjā) because one knows by piercing through with this wisdom. This method applies to all terms. He is called "possessed of true knowledge" (vijjā-sampanna) because he is endowed with the three true knowledges; "possessed of conduct" (caraṇa-sampanna) because he is endowed with the fifteen qualities; and "possessed of true knowledge and conduct" (vijjā-caraṇa-sampanna) because he is endowed with both.
24:
Sanatkumāra refers to the ancient youth, the Brahma who has been known as a youth since a long time ago. It is said that while in the human world, as a youth with five topknots (pañcacūḷaka-kumāra), he attained jhāna and, with his jhāna unimpaired, was reborn in the Brahma world. He was very fond of that particular appearance of his; therefore, he travels about in that same form. Because of that, they recognize him as 'Sanatkumāra'. 'Among the generation' (janetasmiṃ) means among the multitude of beings, among the progeny. 'Those who rely on lineage' (ye gotta-paṭisārino) refers to those among the people who rely on (or are attached to) their lineage, saying, "I am of the Gotama lineage, I am of the Kassapa lineage." Among those in the world who rely on lineage, the khattiya (noble-warrior) is the best. 'Approved by the Blessed One' (anumata bhagavatā) means it was taught by the Blessed One in agreement with my (Ānanda's) explanation of the question. In the Ambaṭṭha Sutta, the Buddha, the Blessed One, said: "Ambaṭṭha, I too say this—

'The khattiya is the best among the generation who rely on lineage,
But one endowed with true knowledge and conduct is the best among gods and humans.'"

By speaking thus, it was authorized and rejoiced in by Him. "Well done, well done, Ānanda"—it is said that the Blessed One, without falling into sleep from the beginning, listened to this sutta and, knowing that Ānanda had brought the practice of the trainee (sekha-paṭipadā) to its peak, He arose, sat down cross-legged, and uttered the words of approval (Sādhu). By this much, this sutta became known as 'spoken by the Victor' (Jinabhāsita). The rest of the words have clear meanings in all places.

## The Commentary on the Sekha Sutta
## in the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished.

## 4. Potaliya Sutta Vaṇṇanā
'Thus have I heard' and so forth is the Potaliya Sutta. Therein, 'among the Aṅguttarāpans' (aṅguttarāpesu) refers to the Aṅga country itself, but because it is not far from the water to the north of the Mahī river, it is also called 'Uttarāpa'. To the north of which Mahī river is the water? It is the water to the north of the Mahā-Mahī river. Here is the explanation regarding that region: This island of Jambudīpa is ten thousand yojanas in extent. Therein, a region four thousand yojanas in extent is covered by water and is designated as the ocean.
25:
He arrived. In an area measuring three thousand yojanas, humans reside. In an area measuring three thousand yojanas, the Himavā mountain is situated. The Himavā mountain is five hundred yojanas in height and is adorned with eighty-four thousand peaks. It is made picturesque by five hundred rivers flowing all around it. In that Himavā mountain, there are seven great lakes: Lake Anotatta, Lake Kaṇṇamuṇḍa, Lake Rathakāra, Lake Chaddanta, Lake Kuṇāla, Lake Mandākinī, and Lake Sīhappapāta, each measuring fifty yojanas in length and fifty yojanas in width, with a circumference of one hundred and fifty yojanas. Among those seven great lakes, Lake Anotatta is surrounded by these five peaks: Sudassana Peak, Citra Peak, Kāḷa Peak, Gandhamādana Peak, and Kelāsa Peak.

Among those peaks, Sudassana Peak is made of gold and is two hundred yojanas in height. It curves inward like a crow's beak and stands covering Lake Anotatta itself. Citra Peak is made of all kinds of jewels. Kāḷa Peak is made of black collyrium stone. Gandhamādana Peak is a plateau, and its interior is the color of green beans. It is abundant with these ten kinds of scents: scent of roots, scent of heartwood, scent of sapwood, scent of bark, scent of bark-flakes (pappaṭika), scent of resin, scent of leaves, scent of flowers (puppha), scent of fruits, and the scent of fragrant trees with all-encompassing aromas; it is covered with various medicinal plants. On the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight, it stands glowing like a mass of burning embers. Kelāsa Peak is made of silver. All these peaks are equal in height and shape to Sudassana Peak, and they stand covering Lake Anotatta itself. All those peaks send down rain through the power of devas and the power of nāgas. Rivers flow from those mountains. All that river water flows only into Lake Anotatta. When the moon and the sun travel either to the south or to the north, they cast light into that lake from between the mountains; however, when they travel directly overhead, they do not cast light. For that reason, the name 'Anotatta' (not heated) arose for that lake.

In that Lake Anotatta, there are delightful stone slabs. Bathing places with water as clear as crystal and free from fish and turtles are well-prepared. At those bathing places, Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, Arahants, and powerful ascetics (isayas) bathe. Devas, yakkhas, and others also enjoy garden sports there.

On the four sides of Lake Anotatta, there are four openings: the Lion's Mouth, the Elephant's Mouth, the Horse's Mouth, and the Bull's Mouth. From these openings, four rivers flow. On the banks of the river emerging from the Lion's Mouth, lions are very numerous. On the banks of the rivers emerging from the Elephant's Mouth and the others, elephants, horses, and bulls are very numerous. The river emerging from the eastern side circles Lake Anotatta three times clockwise, and then, without approaching the other three rivers...
26:
The river emerging from the eastern side circles Lake Anotatta three times clockwise and, without approaching the other three rivers, travels through the Eastern Himavā via a path not frequented by humans and enters the Great Ocean. The rivers emerging from the western and northern sides likewise circle clockwise and travel through the Western Himavā and Northern Himavā respectively via paths not frequented by humans and enter the Great Ocean. However, the river emerging from the southern side circles that lake three times clockwise and then flows straight to the south along a stone plateau for sixty yojanas; hitting a mountain and rising up, it becomes a water column three gāvutas in circumference, travels through the air for sixty yojanas, and falls upon the stone named Tiyaggaḷa. That stone is broken by the force of the water column. In that place, a lake named Tiyaggaḷa, fifty yojanas in size, is formed. Breaking the bank of that lake, the water enters the stone and flows for sixty yojanas. From there, it breaks through the solid earth and travels through a tunnel (umanga) for sixty yojanas; hitting the transverse mountain named Viñjha, it splits into five streams like the five fingers of a palm and flows forth. In the place where that river circles Lake Anotatta three times, it is called Āvaṭṭagaṅgā. In the place where it flows straight along the stone plateau for sixty yojanas, it is called Kaṇhagaṅgā. In the place where it travels through the air for sixty yojanas, it is called Ākāsagaṅgā. In the place where it stays in the fifty-yojana space at the Tiyaggaḷa stone, it is called Tiyaggaḷapokkharaṇī. In the place where it breaks the bank, enters the stone, and flows for sixty yojanas, it is called Bahalagaṅgā. In the place where it flows through the tunnel for sixty yojanas, it is called Umangagaṅgā. In the place where it hits the transverse mountain named Viñjha and flows as five streams, it is known by five names: Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Aciravatī, Sarabhū, and Mahī. Thus, these five great rivers originate from the Himavā mountain. Among those rivers, the fifth one named Mahī is intended here as the Mahāmahī. Because it is not far from the waters to the north of that Mahāmahī river, that region should be known as Anguttarāpa. It is in that Anguttarāpa region.

Regarding the market town named Āpaṇa: in that market town, it is said there were twenty thousand divided shop-fronts. Thus, because of the abundance of shops (āpaṇa), it came to be known simply as Āpaṇa. Near that market town, on the riverbank, there is a large forest grove with dense shade and delightful ground; the Blessed One dwells in that forest grove. Therefore, it should be understood that the specific dwelling place is not strictly defined here. To another forest grove...
27: "tenupasaṅkami" means that after sending the group of monks to their dwelling place, [the Buddha] approached Potaliya the householder alone. "potaliyopi kho gahapati" refers to the householder named Potaliya. "sampannanivāsanapāvuraṇo" means being fully dressed and cloaked. It means wearing one long-fringed cloth and cloaking another. "chattupāhanāhi" means holding a parasol and wearing sandals. "āsanāni" refers to couches, stools, straw stools, and so on. In fact, even a layer of branches is called a seat. "gahapati-vādena" means by the word "householder". "samudācarati" means addressing. "bhagavantaṃ etadavoca" means that Potaliya the householder, unable to endure the word "householder" being used three times, addressed the Blessed One with the words: "Venerable Gotama, this..." and so on. In that speech, "nacchannaṃ" means inappropriate. "nappatirūpaṃ" means unsuitable. All terms such as "ākāra" (aspect) are synonyms denoting cause. Indeed, all the outward appearances of a layman, such as wearing a long-fringed cloth and keeping hair, beard, and nails, are called "ākāra" because they make his status as a layman clear. They are called "liṅga" (mark) because they exist in the form of a layman. They are called "nimitta" (sign) because they are the cause for recognizing the status of a layman. "yathā taṃ gahapatissa" means just as the aspects, marks, and signs of a householder exist, so they exist for you, the householder. Therefore, [the Buddha] shows: "I address you thus as 'householder'." Then, Potaliya the householder, wishing to show why he could not endure being addressed as "householder", said: "Venerable Sir, it is so for me..." and so on. "niyyātaṃ" means relinquished. "anovādī anupavādī" means: one who gives advice in such a way as "Dear ones, plow, plant, engage in trade," etc., is called "ovādī" (an advisor). One who reproaches in such a way as "You do not plow, you do not plant, you do not engage in trade; how will you live, or how will you support your wife and children?" etc., is called "upavādī" (a reproacher). I do neither of those. Therefore, he shows the meaning that he is one who does not advise (anovādī) and does not reproach (anupavādī) those children, lands, and servants. "ghāsacchādanaparamo viharāmi" means living with only food and clothing as the limit. He shows the meaning: "There is nothing beyond this food and clothing, and I do not desire anything more." "giddhilobho pahātabbo" means that greed which has become lust should be abandoned. "anindārosaṃ" means non-offense, which is the opposite of reproach. "nindāroso" means reproach and offense. In the term "vohārasamucchedāya", "vohāra" refers to the usage of trade, the usage of designation, the usage of speech, and the usage of intention. Among those four types of usage—
28:
"Among humans, whoever lives by trade, know him thus, Vāseṭṭha: he is a merchant, not a brahmin" (Majjhima Nikāya). This is called byavahāra-vohāra (business usage). "Enumeration, name, designation, usage" (Dhammasaṅgaṇī). This is called paṇṇatti-vohāra (designation usage). "He speaks in such and such a way without grasping (through craving or views)" (Majjhima Nikāya). This is called vacana-vohāra (speech usage). "Eight noble usages, eight ignoble usages" (Aṅguttara Nikāya). This is called cetanā-vohāra (intentional usage); this intentional usage is intended here.

Alternatively, from the time of becoming a monk, there is no intention (cetanā) of "I am a layman," but only the intention of "I am a monk." There is no speech (vacana) of "layman," but only the speech of "monk." There is no designation (paṇṇatti) of "layman," but only the designation of "monk." There is no business/trade (byavahāra) of "layman," but only the usage (vohāra) of "monk" or "one who has gone forth." Therefore, all these usages are applicable.

"Because of which fetters I am one who takes life"—in this context, killing (pāṇātipāta) itself is the fetter (saṃyojana). It is because of killing that one is called a killer. Because of the plurality of beings, it is said in the plural: "those (fetters)." "Those fetters" refers to those bonds of killing. "Practices for the abandoning and for the cutting off" means practicing for the purpose of abandoning and cutting off by means of the restraint of bodily virtue known as non-killing.

"Even I would reproach myself" means: "Having gone forth in the teaching where one must not take the life of even a louse or an ant, if I cannot refrain from even killing, what is the use of my monkhood?" Thus, it means self-reproach. "The wise, after investigating, would also blame me" means: "Having gone forth in such a teaching, if he cannot refrain from even killing, what is the use of his monkhood?" Thus, other wise and learned people would blame him after weighing and investigating.

In the teaching "This itself is a fetter, this itself is a hindrance," although it is not included among the ten fetters and five hindrances, it is spoken of by way of the teaching of the "eight hindrances." It is called a "fetter" (saṃyojana) in the sense of binding to the round of rebirths, and a "hindrance" (nīvaraṇa) in the sense of obstructing welfare. "Taints" (āsavā) refers to the single taint of ignorance (avijjāsava) arising because of killing. "Distress and fever" (vighātapariḷāhā) refers to suffering and burning.
29:
