Among those two, distress (vighāta) and burning (pariḷāha), by the term 'distress,' both the suffering of defilements (kilesa-dukkha) and the suffering of resultants (vipāka-dukkha) are taken. By the term 'burning,' both the burning of defilements (kilesa-pariḷāha) and the burning of resultants (vipāka-pariḷāha) are taken. In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all sections.

34-40. Specifically, in this phrase 'te sāhaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāya' (for the abandoning of those fetters, I [practice]), the application should be made in all sections as follows: 'I practice for the sake of abandoning, for the sake of total eradication, through the restraint of bodily virtue known as abstaining from taking what is not given; through the restraint of verbal virtue known as truthful speech; through the restraint of verbal virtue known as non-slanderous speech; through the restraint of mental virtue known as being without covetous greed; through the restraint of bodily and verbal virtue known as non-blaming and non-harassing; through the restraint of mental virtue known as non-anger and non-malice; and through the restraint of mental virtue known as being without overbearing conceit.'

In these phrases, 'Even I would reproach myself, and having investigated, the wise would also censure me,' if one, having gone forth in the Dispensation where even a blade of grass or a piece of bamboo should not be taken if not given, is unable to abstain even from taking what is not given, one would reproach oneself: 'What is the use of my monkhood?' The wise, too, having investigated, would censure: 'Having gone forth in such a Dispensation, he is unable to abstain even from taking what is not given; what is the use of this man's monkhood?'

If one, having gone forth in the Dispensation where one should not lie even for the sake of a laugh or for fun, is unable to abstain even from lying, one would reproach oneself: 'What is the use of my monkhood?' The wise, too, having investigated, would censure: 'Having gone forth in such a Dispensation, he is unable to abstain even from lying; what is the use of this man's monkhood?'

If one, having gone forth in the Dispensation where one should not slander in any manner, is unable to abstain even from slandering, one would reproach oneself: 'What is the use of my monkhood?' The wise, too, having investigated, would censure: 'Having gone forth in such a Dispensation, he is unable to abstain even from slandering; what is the use of this man's monkhood?'

If one, having gone forth in the Dispensation where one should not have even a slight amount of covetous greed, is unable to abandon even greed, one would reproach oneself: 'What is the use of my monkhood?' The wise, too, having investigated, would censure: 'Having gone forth in such a Dispensation, he is unable to abandon even greed; what is the use of this man's monkhood?'

If one, having gone forth in the Dispensation where one should not blame or harass others even when one's limbs are being severed with a saw, is unable to abandon even blaming and harassing, one would reproach oneself: 'What is the use of my monkhood?' The wise, too, having investigated, would censure: 'Having gone forth in such a Dispensation, he is unable to abandon even blaming and harassing; what is the use of this man's monkhood?'

If one, having gone forth in the Dispensation where one should not have anger or malice even toward a cut-off stump or a thorn, is unable to abstain even from anger and malice, one would reproach oneself: 'What is the use of my monkhood?' The wise, too, having investigated, would censure: 'Having gone forth in such a Dispensation, he is unable to abstain even from anger and malice; what is the use of this man's monkhood?'

If one, having gone forth in the Dispensation where one should not have overbearing conceit, is unable to abandon even overbearing conceit, one would reproach oneself: 'What is the use of my monkhood?' The wise, too, having investigated, would censure: 'Having gone forth in such a Dispensation, he is unable to abandon even overbearing conceit; what is the use of this man's monkhood?' In this manner, the application should be made in all sections.

In this word 'āsavā' (taints), due to the cause of taking what is not given, three taints arise: the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava), the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava), and the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava). Likewise, due to the cause of lying and the cause of slanderous speech, the three taints—the taint of sensual desire, the taint of views, and the taint of ignorance—arise. Due to the cause of covetous greed, the taint of views...
30:
...and the taint of ignorance arise. Due to the cause of blaming and harassing, only the taint of ignorance arises. Likewise, due to the cause of anger and malice, and due to the cause of overbearing conceit, two taints arise: the taint of existence (bhavāsava) and the taint of ignorance. Thus, the arising of the taints should be understood.

To avoid confusion in these eight sections, here is the summary of the decision: In the first four sections, it is said, 'unable to abstain.' In the latter four sections, it is said, 'unable to abandon.' In killing, blaming/harassing, and anger/malice, only the single taint of ignorance (avijjāsava) occurs. In taking what is not given, lying, and slanderous speech, the taints of sensual desire, views, and ignorance occur. In covetous greed, the taints of views and ignorance occur. In overbearing conceit, the taints of existence and ignorance occur.

Abstaining from killing and taking what is not given are bodily virtue (kāyika-sīla). Truthful speech and non-slanderous speech are verbal virtue (vācasika-sīla). Excluding non-blaming and non-harassing, the remaining three are mental virtue (mānasika-sīla). However, because one strikes or harasses with both body and speech, non-blaming and non-harassing fall into both categories: it is both bodily virtue and verbal virtue. By this much, what is being taught? The virtue of restraint according to the Patimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla). It should be understood that for a monk established in the Patimokkha restraint, the complete cutting off of worldly parlance is taught by way of abandoning through reflection (paṭisaṅkhā-pahāna).

## Commentary on the Talk on the Danger of Sensual Pleasures

In the detailed teaching, the word 'tamenaṃ dakkho' should be understood in connection with the word 'upasumbheyya.' This is what is meant: 'one should throw it to that dog, one should cast it near that dog.' 'Aṭṭhikaṅkala' refers to a breastbone, a backbone, or a skull bone. Because it is fleshless, it is called a skeleton (kaṅkala). 'Sunikkantaṃ nikkantaṃ' means it has been scraped so well that it is completely fleshless, leaving only the bone. Therefore, it is said to be 'nimmamsa' (fleshless). Because it is smeared with blood, it is called 'lohitamakkhita.'

'Bahu-dukkhā bahu-pāyāsā' means there is much suffering due to the pains of this life and the next, and there is much despair due to the defilements of distress. This equanimity, which is of various natures and based on diversity through the power of the five cords of sensual pleasure...
31:
Because of depending on those objects of the five cords of sensual pleasure, the equanimity that arises in the five cords of sensual pleasure is called 'equanimity based on diversity (*nanattasita*)'; excluding that [equanimity]. 'Equanimity based on unity (*ekattasita*)' because of having a single nature refers to the equanimity associated with the fourth jhāna. Indeed, that fourth jhāna equanimity has a single nature because it arises in only one object even for a whole day; because of depending on that single object alone, it is called *ekattasita*.

'Wherein all worldly lures and clingings (*lokāmisu-pādānā*) cease without remainder' means that in the equanimity of the fourth jhāna, by depending on and on account of that fourth jhāna equanimity, the intense lusts having the five cords of sensual pleasure as their object, which are called worldly lures (*lokāmisa*), cease entirely and without remainder. 'Intense lust having the five cords of sensual pleasure as its object (*pañcakāmaguṇāmisa*)' refers to the desire and lust (*chandarāga*) having the five cords of sensual pleasure as their object; because of the sense of firm grasping, those very lusts are also called clingings (*upādāna*). 'He develops that very equanimity' means he develops only that equanimity associated with the fourth jhāna, which is the opposite of worldly lures and clingings.

'Would fly up (*uḍḍīyeyya*)' means to fly up and go. 'Following (*anupatitvā*)' means pursuing. 'Would peck (*vitaccheyyuṃ*)' means biting and pecking with the beak. 'Would drop (*vissajjeyyuṃ*)' means pulling a piece of meat with claws and dropping it.

'A vehicle fit for a man (*yānaṃ vā poriseyyaṃ*)' means a vehicle suitable for a man. 'Noble gems and earrings (*pavaramani-kuṇဍalaṃ*)' means various kinds of noble gems and earrings. 'They take their own goods (*sāni haranti*)' means taking one's own property.

'Having sweet fruit (*sampannaphala*)' means a tree with sweet fruit. 'Abounding in fruit (*upappannaphala*)' means a tree that is full of fruit or has many fruits.

'Unsurpassed (*anuttara*)' means the Dhamma which is noble, radiant, and free from defilements.

'Venerable Sir, I stand at a very great distance' means I am at a very great distance, like the sky from the earth, or like the far shore from the near shore of the ocean. 'One who does not know the reason (*anājānīya*)' means not knowing the reason for cutting off the designation of 'layperson.' 'Food to be eaten by those who know the reason (*ājānīya-bhojana*)' means food to be eaten by good monks who know the reason. 'Food to be eaten by those who do not know the reason (*anājānīya-bhojana*)' means food to be eaten by us wanderers who do not know the reason. The remaining words are clear in meaning in all places.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Potalia Sutta is finished.
32:
## 5. Commentary on the Jīvaka Sutta
This sutta beginning with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' is the Jīvaka Sutta. In that Jīvaka Sutta, in the phrase 'Jīvakassa komārabhaccassa ambavane,' he is called 'Jīvaka' because it was said 'he still lives (*jīvati*).' He is called 'Komārabhacca' because it was said 'he was nourished by the prince (*kumārena bhato*).' Regarding this matter, when it was asked, 'Friends, what is that surrounded by crows?', they replied, 'It is a child, O Prince.' When asked, 'Friends, does he still live?', they replied, 'He still lives, O Prince.' Therefore, he commanded, 'Friends, if so, take that child to the inner palace and give him to the nurses to be raised.' They gave the child the name 'Jīvaka' because it was said 'he still lives.' They gave him the name 'Komārabhacca' because he was caused to be raised by Prince Abhaya (as stated in the Mahāvagga). This is just a summary here. The details should be known as they appear in the Khandhaka of the Vinaya Mahāvagga. The decision regarding this Jīvaka has also been stated in the Samantapāsādikā, the Vinaya Commentary.

This Jīvaka, on one occasion, treated the Buddha's body which was afflicted by a disorder (illness) with a purgative, and after offering a pair of Sīveyyaka cloths, he was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*) at the end of the thanksgiving for the robes. Then he thought, 'I must go to attend upon the Buddha two or three times a day; this Veḷuvana monastery is very far, but my mango grove is much closer. It would be good if I were to build a monastery for the Blessed One in this mango grove.' That Jīvaka, having prepared night quarters, day quarters, caves, cells, pavilions, and so on in that mango grove, and having built a fragrant hut (*gandhakuṭi*) suitable for the Blessed One, had the mango grove enclosed by a wall eighteen cubits high and the color of a copper plate. Having satisfied the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha with robes and alms-food, he poured the water of dedication and donated the monastery. It is in reference to this donation that it was said, 'In the mango grove of Jīvaka Komārabhacca.'

'They kill (*ārabhanti*)' means they slaughter. 'Specifically prepared (*uddisakataṃ*)' means (meat) prepared specifically for (someone). 'Action on account of (*paṭiccakammaṃ*)' means (meat) prepared on account of oneself. Alternatively, 'paṭiccakamma' is a designation for the root action of taking life (*pāṇātipāta-kamma*). Because there is an act of taking life on account of that person in this meat, the meat is called 'paṭiccakamma.' One who consumes such meat is also an heir to that kamma; just as the act of taking life occurs for the killer, so too the act of taking life occurs for the one who eats that meat knowingly—this is the view of those heretics (*titthiyas*). 'They explain according to the Dhamma (*dhammassa cānudhammaṃ vyākaronti*)' means they speak of the secondary reason (*anukāraṇa*) which is suitable for the primary reason (*kāraṇa*) spoken by the Blessed One. Here, the primary reason (*kāraṇa*) refers to the consumption of fish and meat that is pure in three respects (*tikoṭiparisuddha*). The secondary reason (*anukāraṇa*) refers to answering the multitude in that same way. However, since the Blessed One does not consume meat specifically prepared for him, the eating of such meat is not the primary reason (*kāraṇa*), nor is the heretics' explanation in such a manner the secondary reason (*anukāraṇa*)...
33:
Answering is not a suitable reason. Regarding 'a legitimate doctrine or counter-doctrine,' does there not exist even a slight fault, which wise people would blame, in your doctrine or counter-doctrine that others have stated with reason? This means: "Is there no reason for blame in your doctrine in every respect?" *Abbhācikkhanti* means they speak by overpowering.

*Ṭhānehi* means by reasons. Among 'seen' and so on, 'seen' (*diṭṭha*) refers to meat where one has seen animals being killed and taken for the benefit of monks. 'Heard' (*suta*) refers to meat where one has heard that animals were killed and taken for the benefit of monks. 'Suspected' (*parisaṅkita*) is of three kinds: suspected through seeing, suspected through hearing, and suspected independently of both.

In these three kinds of suspicion, the comprehensive decision is as follows: In this Sasana, monks see people leaving the village or wandering in the forest with nets, traps, and so on in their hands. On the second day, when those monks enter that village for alms, people bring alms-food together with fish and meat. Because of what they saw, those monks suspect, "Was this prepared for the benefit of the monks?" This is called 'suspected through seeing' (*diṭṭhaparisaṅkita*). It is not proper to accept such suspected meat. However, it is proper to accept meat that is not so suspected. If those people ask, "Venerable sirs, why do you not accept it?" and upon hearing the reason, they say, "Venerable sirs, this was not prepared for the monks; it was prepared for ourselves or for government officials," then it is allowable to accept it.

Monks do not see, but they hear, "It is said that people are leaving the village or wandering in the forest with nets, traps, and so on in their hands." On the second day, when those monks enter that village for alms, people bring alms-food together with fish and meat. Because of what they heard, those monks suspect, "Was this prepared for the benefit of the monks?" This is called 'suspected through hearing' (*sutaparisaṅkita*). It is not proper to accept this meat. However, it is proper to accept meat that is not so suspected. If those people ask, "Venerable sirs, why do you not accept it?" and upon hearing the reason, they say, "Venerable sirs, this was not prepared for the monks; it was prepared for ourselves or for government officials," then it is allowable to accept it.

They neither see nor hear, yet when those monks enter the village for alms, people take their bowls, prepare alms-food with fish and meat, and bring it to them. Those monks suspect, "Was this prepared for the benefit of the monks?" This kind of suspicion is called 'suspected independently of both seeing and hearing' (*tadubhayavimuttaparisaṅkita*). It is also not proper to accept this suspected meat. Meat that is not so suspected...
34:
...is allowable. If those people ask, "Venerable sirs, why do you not accept it?" and upon hearing the reason for suspicion, they say, "Venerable sirs, this meat was not prepared for the monks; it was prepared for ourselves or for the king's ministers and so on; or it is meat already available (*pavattamaṃsa*); we obtained only allowable meat and prepared it for the monks," then it is allowable.

The same method should be noted for meals prepared for the dead (*matakabhatta*) or for auspicious ceremonies (*maṅgala*), and so on. Whatever meat is not prepared specifically for monks, and where they are free from doubt, all such meat is allowable. If it is prepared for the monks residing in a certain monastery, and those monks do not know it was prepared for them, but other monks know; it is not allowable for the monks who know, but it is allowable for those who do not know. If others do not know, but only the intended monks know; it is not allowable only for those who know, but it is allowable for the others. If the intended monks know, "It was prepared for us," and other monks also know, "It was prepared for them," then that meat is not allowable for all of them. If none of them know, it is allowable for all. Indeed, if it is prepared specifically for any one of the five types of fellow practitioners (*sahadhammika*), it is not allowable for all fellow practitioners.

If someone kills a living being specifically for one monk and fills that monk's bowl to offer it, and that monk, while knowing it was prepared for him, accepts it and gives it to another monk, and that other monk consumes it out of faith in the donor monk; if it is asked, "Which monk incurs an offense?" neither monk incurs an offense. This is because for the monk for whom it was prepared, there is no offense as he did not eat it; for the other monk, there is no offense because he did not know. Indeed, there is no offense in accepting allowable meat. For a monk who eats meat prepared specifically for him without knowing it, there is no such thing as the duty of confessing an offense even if he finds out later. However, a monk who eats unallowable meat (*akappiyamamsa*) without knowing it must confess the offense even if he finds out later. Indeed, an offense is incurred only for one who eats meat knowing it was prepared specifically for him; but for unallowable meat, an offense is incurred even for one who eats it without knowing. Therefore, a monk who is afraid of offenses should accept meat only after inquiring, even while noting the appearance of the meat; or he should accept it with the intention, "I will inquire and consume it at the time of use," and then consume it only after inquiring. Why? Because it is difficult to distinguish. Bear meat resembles pork, and leopard meat and so on resemble venison; therefore, the teachers say that it is proper to accept only after inquiring.

'Not seen' (*adiṭṭha*) means not seeing the meat being killed and taken for the monks. 'Not heard' (*asuta*) means not hearing that it was killed and taken for the monks. 'Not suspected' (*aparisaṅkita*) means having no suspicion through reasons such as seeing or hearing. "I say it is to be consumed" means that meat which is pure in these three aspects is called 'pure in three aspects' (*tikoṭiparisuddha*). Consuming such meat is like consuming vegetable curry grown in the forest. For one consuming such meat...
35:
It means: "For a monk who dwells in loving-kindness, there is no fault or blame; therefore, I say that such (pure) meat should be consumed."

Now, to show the faultlessness of a monk dwelling in loving-kindness when consuming such (pure) meat, the Buddha said: "Jīvaka, here [in this Dispensation], a monk..." and so forth. In this statement, although the word "monk" is used without specification, it should be understood that the Buddha was referring specifically to himself. Indeed, in these three places—the Mahāvacchagotta Sutta, the Caṅkī Sutta, and this Jīvaka Sutta—the Buddha gave the teaching referring to himself. Regarding "with exquisite alms-food": in the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta below, any expensive alms-food is intended as "exquisite alms-food," but in this sutta, only alms-food mixed with meat is intended. "Agathito" means not being tied by craving. "Amucchito" means not being infatuated by the infatuation of craving. "Anajjhopanno" means not being overwhelmed; it means not being like a crow that wants to swallow the entire lump of food in one go. "Ādīnavadassāvī" means seeing the danger in such a way as: "having stayed for one night and entered the stomach, it will exit through the nine orifices (wounds)," and so on. "Nissaraṇapañño paribhuñjati" means consuming after discerning with wisdom that "this consumption of food is for the purpose of maintaining this body," and so forth. "He intends for his own affliction" means he intends for his own suffering. "I have heard this before" shows: "I have heard this in the past; this is merely something I have heard." "Jīvaka, if you spoke referring to this" means: "Jīvaka, the Great Brahma has abandoned ill-will and so forth through abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna), therefore he is called one who dwells in loving-kindness. I have abandoned them through abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna). If you spoke referring to this abandonment by eradication, then I accept these words of yours." Jīvaka then acknowledged this.

Then, the Buddha, wishing to further expand the teaching to Jīvaka by way of the remaining brahmavihāras, said: "Jīvaka, here, a monk..." and so forth. That statement has an obvious meaning.

"Jīvaka, he who..." is a separate connection (anusandhi). In this place, the Buddha closes the door [of blame] and shows compassion for beings. If someone were to think: "By offering a single meal of delicious alms-food, one can obtain the bliss of heaven for a hundred thousand aeons; therefore, by whatever unwholesome means or even by killing another, one should offer only delicious alms-food," the Buddha, wishing to prohibit such a thought, said: "Jīvaka, he who [intends for the Tathāgata]..." and so forth.
36:
In that passage, "by this first ground" means by this first cause, which is merely the act of giving an order. "Causing the neck to tremble" means being tied by the neck with a rope and pulled, causing the neck to tremble. "When being killed" means being slaughtered. "Offends with unallowable meat" means feeding someone bear meat as pork, or leopard meat as venison, and then mocking them by saying, "How can you be called a monk? You have eaten unallowable meat." However, for those who, during times of famine or for the purpose of curing a disease, know that "bear meat is similar to pork, and leopard meat is similar to venison," and say, "This is pork, this is venison," feeding them with a beneficial intention—this was not said referring to them. For such people, much merit indeed accrues. The one who says, "Venerable Sir, I go to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha for refuge," is the noble disciple Jīvaka, who has attained the fruit, understood the Dispensation, and seen the Truth. However, entering into this Dhamma teaching, he spoke thus to express his devotion and to praise the Dhamma talk. The rest is clear in all places.

## The Explanation of the Jīvaka Sutta
## in the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya named Papañcasūdanī is finished.
## 6. Explanation of the Upāli Sutta

"Thus have I heard" and so forth is the Upāli Sutta. In that sutta, "at Nālandā" means in the city named Nālandā, dwelling there making that city his resort for alms. "In Pāvārika’s Mango Grove" means in the mango grove of the wealthy cloth merchant Pāvārika. It is said that this was his park; having heard the Buddha's Dhamma teaching and gaining confidence in the Buddha, he built a monastery in that park, adorned with huts, caves, pavilions, and so forth, and offered it to the Buddha. That monastery became known as "Pāvārikambavana," just like Jīvaka’s Mango Grove. It means he dwells in that Pāvārika Mango Grove. "Dīghatapassī" is a Nigaṇṭha who received this name because of his tall stature. "Having returned from the alms-round" means having come back from seeking alms. If one asks whether the term "piṇḍapāta" (alms-food) exists in external sects as it does in the Dispensation, the answer is no.

"Paññapeti" means he shows or lays down. "He lays down punishments"—this was said by the Buddha wishing to ask according to the Nigaṇṭha doctrine. Regarding "bodily punishment, verbal punishment, and mental punishment," the Nigaṇṭhas lay down the first two punishments as being without mind (acittaka). Just as a branch moves when the wind blows, or water moves, and there is no mind in that branch or water, so too, bodily punishment is likewise without mind. To speak of verbal punishment: when the wind blows, palm leaves and so forth make a sound, and water makes a sound; in those palm leaves and water, the mind...
37:
Water moves, but there is no mind in it; in this way, the body-rod (kāyadaṇḍa) is also mindless. Just as when the wind blows, palm leaves and such make sound, or as water makes sound, and there is no mind in that sound-making; similarly, the speech-rod (vacīdaṇḍa) is also mindless. Thus, these two rods are designated as mindless things. The mind, however, is designated as the mind-rod (manodaṇḍa). Then, the Blessed One, wishing to establish the words of Dīgha Tapassī, said: "Tapassī, how is it?" and so forth.

In that context, "kathāvatthusmiṃ" means within the talk itself. It means He established him in the talk. Why did the Blessed One do this? Because the Blessed One saw: "This Dīgha Tapassī will take these words and go to report them to his teacher, the Great Nigaṇṭha. In that Nigaṇṭha's assembly, Upāli the householder is sitting. Upāli the householder, having heard these words, will come to refute me. To him, I shall preach the Dhamma. He will take refuge three times. At that time, I shall reveal the Four Noble Truths to him. At the end of the revelation of the Truths, he will be established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala). Indeed, I have fulfilled the Perfections (pāramīs) only for the sake of helping others." Seeing this special benefit, He acted in this way.

"He designated actions (kammas)"—the Nigaṇṭha said this, wishing to ask according to the Buddha's doctrine. Among these three—bodily action, verbal action, and mental action—the twenty volitions (cetanā), consisting of the eight wholesome volitions of the sense sphere and the twelve unwholesome volitions, which reach the state of taking, grasping, rubbing, or moving at the body-door, are called bodily action (kāyakamma). Those same twenty volitions, when they do not reach taking and so forth at the body-door but reach the breaking of speech at the speech-door, are called verbal action (vacīkamma). The twenty-nine wholesome and unwholesome volitions that occur at the mind-door without reaching movement in either of the two doors are called mental action (manokamma). Alternatively, in brief, the three types of bodily misconduct are called bodily action; the four types of verbal misconduct are called verbal action; and the three types of mental misconduct are called mental action.

In this Upāli Sutta, action (kamma) is the primary focus (dhura). Although in the subsequent Kukkuravatika Sutta it is mentioned as, "Puṇṇa, these four actions have been realized and declared by me through my own higher knowledge," volition (cetanā) is the primary focus there. Volition occurring at any door receives classifications such as "dark action with dark result," and so forth. In the Niddesa section, that same volition is spoken of in such ways as, "He performs a bodily formation (kāyasaṅkhāra) accompanied by suffering." However, in this sutta, volition occurring at the body-door is intended as bodily action.
38:
Volition occurring at the speech-door is called verbal action (vacīkamma); volition occurring at the mind-door is called mental action (manokamma). Therefore, it is said: "In this sutta, action (kamma) is the primary focus, while in the subsequent sutta, volition (cetanā) is the primary focus." Indeed, the Blessed One designates action as action even in this very sutta. Regarding volition, He also taught: "Monks, I say that volition is action; having willed, one performs an action through body, speech, or mind." Why is volition called action? Because action has volition as its root.

In this matter, regarding unwholesome (akusala) acts, one does not err in saying that bodily action and verbal action are great; regarding wholesome (kusala) acts, one does not err in saying that mental action is great. This is because the four [heinous] actions such as matricide (mātughātaka) are initiated and performed only by the body. However, the action of causing a schism in the Saṅgha (saṅghabhedaka), which results in remaining in hell for an aeon, is performed through the speech-door. Thus, one who says that bodily and verbal actions are great regarding unwholesome acts is said to be not in error. On the other hand, a single volition of meditative absorption (jhāna-cetanā) can bring about the bliss of heavenly and Brahma realms for eighty-four thousand aeons. A single volition of the Path (magga-cetanā) can eradicate all unwholesome states and lead to the attainment of Arahantship. Thus, one who says that mental action is great regarding wholesome acts is said to be not in error. However, in this context, when the Blessed One says that mental action is most blameworthy regarding unwholesome acts, He is speaking with reference to fixed wrong view (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi). Therefore, He said: "Monks, I do not see even a single other thing that is so greatly blameworthy as this, namely, monks, wrong view. Monks, wrong views are the most greatly blameworthy of all."

Now, the Nigaṇṭha, though wishing to follow the path taken by the Tathāgata but seeing no successful outcome, said: "How is it, friend Gotama?" and so forth.

Regarding "Bālakiniyā," it is said that Upāli had a village named Bālakaloṇakāra. People had come from there after collecting taxes. That Upāli the householder said, "Come, friends, let us go see our teacher, the Great Nigaṇṭha," and went there surrounded by that assembly. With reference to that journey, it is said, "bālakiniyā parisāyā," meaning the assembly residing in Bālaka village. "Upālipamukhāyā" means the assembly led by Upāli the householder. Alternatively, "Bālakiniyā" means an assembly full of fools (bāla). "Upālipamukhāyā" is said because only Upāli the householder in that assembly possessed some wisdom, and he was the leader and chief of that assembly of fools. "Handa" is an indeclinable used as a sentence-linker. "Chavo" means vile or low. "Oḷārikassa" means great (intended in comparison with the body-rod)...
39:
To the great (bodily rod). 'Upadhāya' means having placed nearby. This is what is meant: having placed it near the bodily rod, when one looks and compares, 'Is this rod great? Is that rod great?', how can the inferior mental rod shine? From where would it shine? It does not shine. It is shown that it is not even sufficient for mere comparison. Giving a blessing to Dīgha Tapassī, saying 'Sadhu, sadhu, Venerable Tapassī,' he addresses Nāṭaputta as 'Venerable Sir.'

'Venerable Sir, I do not approve of this (Upāli the householder's going)' means 'Venerable Sir, this matter is not pleasing to me.' 'Māyāvī' means a deceiver (a magician). 'Āvaṭṭanimāyaṃ' refers to the art (magic) of turning back and capturing (the mind). 'Āvaṭṭeti' means capturing by encircling. Why does the Great Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta send Upāli the householder up to three times, saying 'Householder, you go'? Why does Dīgha Tapassī repeatedly forbid it? The reason is that although the Great Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta lived in the same city as the Blessed One, he had never seen the Blessed One before. One who claims to be a teacher (a Buddha) cannot see the true Buddha without abandoning that claim. Therefore, because this Great Nigaṇṭha had never seen the Buddha before, and did not know the perfection of seeing the Dasabala (the Ten-Powered One) and the nature of His emancipating talk, he sent him three times. Dīgha Tapassī, however, had from time to time approached the Blessed One, stood, sat, and asked questions; thus he knew the perfection of seeing the Tathāgata and the nature of His emancipating talk. Then Dīgha Tapassī thought: 'This Upāli the householder is a wise man; if he goes to the ascetic Gotama, he might become devoted just by seeing him, or he might become devoted upon hearing the emancipating talk. If he becomes devoted, he will not come back to us again.' Therefore, he forbade it three times.

'Abhivādetvā' means having paid homage. Generally, whether they are devoted or not, most people pay homage when they see the Blessed One; only a few do not. Why? Because even if He were a householder, being born in an extremely noble family, He would still be worthy of homage. But this householder paid homage out of devotion; it is said he became devoted just by seeing Him. 'Āgamā nu khvidha' should be broken down as 'Āgamā nu kho idha' (Has he come here?).

Giving a blessing to Dīgha Tapassī, saying 'Sadhu, sadhu, Venerable Tapassī,' he addresses the Blessed One as 'Venerable Sir.' 'Sacce patiṭṭhāya' means standing on the truth of speech, like a post driven into a heap of chaff that remains unshaken. 'Siyā no' means 'it would be for us.'
40:
'Idha' means in this world. 'Assa' means it would be. 'Sītodakapaṭikkhitto' means the Nigaṇṭhas reject cold water with the perception that it contains living beings; this is said with reference to that rejection. The devas called 'Manosatta' are those attached and clinging to the mind. 'Manopaṭibaddho' shows that because one dies while being attached to the mind, one is reborn among the Manosatta devas. That person will have a bilious fever. Therefore, it is not suitable to bring him hot water for drinking, for washing hands and feet, or for sprinkling on the body; the disease would become stronger. Only cold water is suitable; it calms the disease. However, this Nigaṇṭha uses only hot water; if he does not get hot water, he uses sour rice gruel. But in his mind, he desires to drink and use cold water. Because of that desire to drink and use cold water, the mental rod (manodaṇḍa) of that Nigaṇṭha breaks right at the moment that thought arises. That Nigaṇṭha, thinking 'I will guard the bodily rod and the verbal rod,' does not dare to say 'Give me only cold water' even though he wants to drink and use it. The bodily and verbal rods thus guarded are unable to pull one toward death or rebirth. But the mental rod, even though broken, is indeed able to pull one toward death and rebirth. Thus, the Blessed One made him admit: 'The weak bodily and verbal rods are inferior; only the mental rod is powerful and great.'

That lay follower also had this thought: 'Beings who are unconscious due to fainting do not have inhalation and exhalation even for seven days, yet they are not called dead just because the continuity of the mind persists. When the mind no longer persists for them, only then do they reach the state where it should be said, "These people are dead; take them out of the house and cremate them." The bodily rod has no effort or activity; the verbal rod is the same. It is only through the mind that death and rebirth occur for those beings. Thus, the mental rod alone is great. Even when broken, because it pulls one toward death and rebirth, this mental rod alone is great. The words of our Great Nigaṇṭha are not emancipating,' he reflected. However, wishing to hear the Blessed One's diverse and brilliant answers to questions, he did not yet concede.

'Na kho te sandhiyati' means it does not tally for you. 'Purimena vā pacchimaṃ' means the former statement 'the bodily rod is great' does not tally with the current statement 'the mental rod is great.' 'Pacchimena vā purimaṃ' means that latter statement does not tally with that former statement.
41:
## Now, the Blessed One, wishing to present other reasons to Upāli the householder, spoke the words beginning with, "What do you think of this?" In those words, "one who is restrained by the fourfold restraint" means one who does not kill a living being himself, does not cause others to kill, and does not approve of one who kills. He does not take what is not given himself, does not cause others to take it, and does not approve of one who takes it. He does not speak falsehood himself, does not cause others to speak it, and does not approve of one who speaks it. He does not long for the five cords of sensual pleasure himself, does not cause others to long for them, and does not approve of one who longs for them. Thus, he is restrained by this fourfold restraint. Here, "bhāvita" refers to the five cords of sensual pleasure.

"One who has warded off all water" means one who has avoided all cold water. This is because that Nigantha perceives living beings in cold water and therefore does not use it. Alternatively, "one who has warded off all water" means one whose evil is warded off by the warding off of all evil. "One who is endowed with all warding" means one who is endowed with the warding off of all evil. "One who has shaken off all evil by warding" means one whose evil is shaken off by the warding off of all evil. "One who is suffused with all warding" means one who is suffused with the warding off of all evil. "He causes the destruction of small insects" means he commits the killing of small creatures. It is said that he designates a living being as a one-sensed being or a two-sensed being. He designates even dry wood, old leaves, gravel, and potsherds as living beings. In that regard, he perceives a small drop of water as a small living being and a large one as a large living being. It was in reference to such perceptions that this was said. "Where does he designate it?" is a question asking in which category he designates it. "He designates it in the rod of mind (manodaṇḍa), Bhante," he replied. While speaking, this householder Upāli himself noted: "Our Great Nigantha designates unintentional action as having little blame and intentional action as having great blame, and then designates intention as the rod of mind. This talk of the Nigantha does not lead to deliverance (aniyyānika); only the word of the Blessed One leads to deliverance (niyyānika)."

"Iddha" means prosperous. "Phīta" means extremely prosperous, like being in full bloom. "Crowded with people" means teeming with various kinds of people. "Pāṇa" (living beings) refers to animals such as elephants and horses, as well as human beings such as women, men, and children. "A single heap of meat" means a single mass of flesh. The word "puñja" is a synonym for that word "khala." "One possessed of psychic power" means one endowed with majesty. "One who has attained mastery over the mind" means one who is capable of training the mind. "I shall turn it into ashes" means I will make it a heap of ashes. What the householder Upāli meant by saying, "How could this city of Nāḷandā not become a single heap of meat and yet remain beautiful?" was this: Even if fifty men were to make a physical effort, they could not make the city of Nāḷandā a single heap of meat; however, a single person with psychic power and mastery of the mind could turn it into ashes with a single thought of anger. He thought, "The talk of our Nigantha does not lead to deliverance; only the word of the Blessed One leads to deliverance."
42:
A single person is able to turn [a city] into ashes with just a single instance of mental corruption (anger). "The talk of our Great Nigantha does not lead to deliverance; only the talk of the Blessed One leads to deliverance," Upāli noted.

"Aranyaṃ aranyabhūtaṃ" means becoming a forest in the sense of being a mere forest without any villages. "By the mental corruption of the sages (Isis)" means that the deities, unable to endure the mental anger of the sages directed toward them, destroyed those kingdoms. Worldly people, however, think, "The sages corrupted their minds and destroyed them." Therefore, it should be understood that this assertion of the doctrine was made by standing only on this worldly parlance.

In that regard, the manner in which the kingdoms of King Daṇḍakī and others became forests should be known as follows: When the retinue of the Sarabhaṅga Bodhisatta had become very large, a sage named Kisavaccha, a disciple of the Great Being, desiring to live in solitude, left the group. He departed from the banks of the Godhāvarī River and, depending on the city named Kumbhapura of King Daṇḍakī in the Kalinga country, dwelt in the royal garden developing solitude. The general was his attendant.

At that time, a certain courtesan, riding a chariot and surrounded by five hundred women, went about beautifying the city. The great multitude went about surrounding and looking only at that courtesan, so that the city streets were not wide enough. The king, standing and opening the window, saw her and asked, "Who is this?" "She is the courtesan who beautifies your city, O King," the ministers replied. The king, being envious, said, "How can it be beautiful because of this woman? The city will be beautiful by itself," and he had her position (rank) revoked.

From then on, that courtesan, having made friends with someone and seeking to regain her position, entered the royal garden one day. Seeing the sage sitting on a stone slab near the resting board at the end of the walkway, she thought: "Indeed, this sage is dirty; he is not anointed or adorned. His face is covered with a long beard, his chest is covered with hair, and hair has grown long in both his armpits." Then, dissatisfaction arose in that woman: "I am going about on a certain business, and I have seen this ill-omen (kāḷakaṇṇī). Bring water; I will wash my eyes." Saying so, she had water and a tooth-stick brought. After chewing the tooth-stick, she spat lumps of saliva onto the sage's body, threw the tooth-stick onto his matted hair, washed her face, and [poured] the rinsing water right onto the sage's head...
43:
(The courtesan) washed her eyes and departed, saying, "With these eyes, I have seen a wretch; those eyes are now washed, and the misfortune has been removed."

On that very day, King Daṇḍakī regained his mindfulness and asked, "Friends, where is the city-belle?" When they replied, "Great King, she is in this very city," he ordered her position to be restored, saying, "Give her back her original rank." Although she regained her position due to her previous meritorious deeds, she believed it was because she had spat on the ascetic's body.

A few days later, the King took away the position of the royal chaplain. The chaplain went to the courtesan and asked, "Sister, what did you do to regain your position?" She replied, "Brahmin, what else is there to do? In the royal garden, there is a deceitful ascetic, an un-anointed wretch. Spit on his body, and you will regain your position." The chaplain agreed, saying, "Very well, sister," went there, did exactly as she said, and left. On that same day, King Daṇḍakī regained his mindfulness and asked, "Friends, where is the chaplain?" When they replied, "Great King, he is in this very city," the King ordered, "We acted without due consideration; give that Brahmin back his position." The chaplain also regained it through the power of his merit but believed, "I got it because I spat on the ascetic's body."

A few days later, a rebellion broke out at the King's borders, and he became angry. Thinking, "I will suppress the border rebellion," the King set out with his fourfold army. The chaplain went and stood before the King, saying, "May the Great King be victorious!" and asked, "Great King, are you marching for the sake of victory?" "Yes, Brahmin," the King replied. "If that is so," the chaplain said, "there is a deceitful ascetic, an un-anointed wretch, living in the royal garden. Spit on his body and then depart." Taking the foolish Brahmin's advice, the King did exactly what the courtesan and the chaplain had done. He then commanded his harem, "Spit on the body of this deceitful ascetic." Then the harem ladies and their attendants did the same.

Furthermore, the King stationed guards at the garden gate and issued an order: "No one departing with the King shall leave the garden without spitting on the ascetic's body." Then the entire host of soldiers and officials, following that same rule, threw spit, tooth-sticks, and mouth-wash water upon the ascetic. Spit and tooth-sticks covered his entire body.
44:
When the General, who was at the very rear, heard of this, his heart was troubled, thinking, "They have thus insulted my teacher, the venerable one, the field of merit, and the stairway to heaven." Sighing deeply, he hurried to the royal garden. Seeing the ascetic in such a state of ruin, he tied his waistband firmly, cleared away the tooth-sticks with both hands, lifted him up, and seated him in a suitable place. He then had water brought, bathed him, anointed his body with all kinds of medicines and the four types of perfumes, rubbed him with a fine cloth, and stood before him with joined palms, asking, "Venerable sir, the people have done what is improper; what will be the consequence for them?" The deities were divided into three groups: some said, "We will destroy only the King"; some said, "We will destroy the King along with his retinue"; and others said, "We will destroy the King's entire realm." Despite this, the ascetic did not feel even the slightest anger. Wishing only to show the way to peace for the world, he said, "Offenses are bound to happen; however, for one who knows how to confess and ask for forgiveness, things can be restored to their original state."

Having found a way to avert the danger, the General went to the King, paid homage, and said, "Great King, you have committed a grave deed by offending a guiltless and powerful ascetic. The deities are divided into three groups and are saying such things." After reporting everything, he added, "Great King, if you ask for forgiveness, things can be restored to normal. Do not destroy the country; please ask the ascetic for forgiveness." Although the King saw the fault he had committed, he said, "I will not ask that ascetic for forgiveness." The General pleaded up to three times, but the King was unwilling. The General then said, "Great King, I know the power of the ascetic. He is not one who speaks untruth, nor is he angry. He says this only out of compassion for living beings. Great King, please ask him for forgiveness." "I will not," the King replied. "In that case," the General said, "give the position of General to someone else; I will no longer live within the sphere of your authority." "Go wherever you wish," the King said, "I shall find another General for myself." Then the General went to the ascetic, paid homage, and asked, "Venerable sir, how should I proceed?" The ascetic replied, "General, take everyone who listens to your words, along with their requisites, wealth, and two-footed and four-footed animals, and go beyond the borders of the kingdom within seven days. The deities are exceedingly angry and will surely turn this kingdom into a non-kingdom, destroying it." The General did as instructed.

As soon as the King had gone, he crushed his enemies, pacified the province, and upon his return, stayed at the victory camp, had the city prepared, and then entered the city.
45:
The deities first caused a rain of water to fall. The multitude was delighted, thinking, "Since the time our king offended the deceitful ascetic, there has only been prosperity for our king; he has crushed his enemies, and on the very day of his arrival, it rained." The deities then caused a rain of jasmine flowers to fall, and the multitude was even more delighted. The deities then caused a rain of beans (māsa) to fall. After that, a rain of coins (kahāpaṇa). Then, the deities, thinking that the people should not have to go outside to pick up the coins, caused a rain of valuable goods such as jewelry to fall within reach of their hands and feet. Even those on the seven-storied palace descended, adorned themselves with the ornaments, and were delighted. They uttered joyful words, saying, "Spitting on the deceitful ascetic was indeed worthy! Since the time of spitting on him, prosperity has come to our king, enemies have been crushed, it rained on the day of his return, and then four kinds of rain occurred: jasmine rain, bean rain, coin rain, and ornament rain." Thus, they approved of the evil deed committed by the king.

At that time, the deities rained down various weapons, such as single-edged and double-edged ones, upon the multitude, as if chopping meat on a board. After that, a rain of glowing coals, flameless and smokeless, the color of Butea flowers. After that, a rain of stones the size of gabled houses. After that, they caused a rain of fine sand that could not be held in a fist, creating a mound eighty cubits high. In the king's realm, only three human beings remained unharmed: the ascetic Kisavaccha, the general, and Rāma, who cared for his mother. For the remaining animals who were not involved in that deed, there was no water where there should be water, and no grass where there should be grass. As those animals went in search of water and grass, they reached the borders of the kingdom on the seventh day before arriving at their destination. Therefore, the Sarabhaṅga Bodhisatta said:

"Because King Daṇḍakī insulted the ascetic Kisavaccha by spitting on him,
He, along with his relatives and his kingdom, was uprooted;
He is being cooked in the hell named Kukkula,
And sparks of fire fall upon his body."

Thus should be known how King Daṇḍakī's kingdom turned into a forest.
46:
While King Nāḷikīra was reigning in the Kaliṅga kingdom, five hundred ascetics lived in the Himalayas. They were free from the scent of women, wore antelope skins, had matted hair, wore bark garments, and lived on forest roots and fruits. After living there for a long time, they descended to human habitations to seek salt and vinegar, and eventually reached the city of King Nāḷikīra in the Kaliṅga kingdom. Having arranged their matted hair, antelope skins, and bark garments, they entered the city for alms, displaying a peaceful grace suitable for renunciants. In a time when no Buddha had yet appeared, the people, seeing the ascetics, were inspired with faith. They prepared seats, took the alms bowls from their hands, invited them to sit, and provided them with ample alms-food. When the ascetics had finished their meal, they gave a blessing (anumodanā). Having heard the Dhamma, the people were filled with faith and asked, "Venerable sirs, where are you going?" When they replied, "Lay followers, we shall go to a place where we can live comfortably," the people requested, "Venerable sirs, do not go elsewhere. Please stay in the royal garden. After we have eaten our morning meal, we will come to the garden to listen to the Dhamma." The ascetics accepted and went to the garden. After eating their morning meal, the citizens dressed in clean clothes and went towards the garden in groups, saying, "We will listen to the Dhamma."

The king, standing on the upper palace, saw the people going like that and asked an attendant, "Friend, why are these citizens dressed in clean clothes and clean upper robes, heading towards the garden? Is there a festival or a play there?" "Your Majesty, there is none. They are going because they wish to hear the Dhamma from the ascetics." "Friend, if that is so, I too will go. Let them go with me." The attendant went and told the people, "Our King also wishes to go. Go only after surrounding the King." The citizens were naturally delighted, and hearing this, they were even more pleased, thinking, "Our king is faithless, without devotion, and immoral. The ascetics are righteous. By relying on them, the king too will become righteous." The king left the city, surrounded by the people, went to the garden, exchanged pleasantries with the ascetics, and sat on one side. Seeing the king, the ascetics signaled to one ascetic who was skilled in discourse, "Preach the Dhamma to the king." That ascetic, looking at the assembly, preached on the danger of the five enmities and the benefits of the five precepts:

One should not kill living beings, one should not take what is not given, one should not commit sexual misconduct, one should not speak falsehoods, and one should not drink intoxicants. Killing living beings (pāṇātipāta) leads to rebirth in hell, in the animal realm, or in the realm of hungry ghosts. Likewise, taking what is not given and the others also lead to hell, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts. When the karma of killing living beings has been suffered in hell and one returns to the human realm, it causes a short life due to the remaining result. Taking what is not given, when one returns to the human realm after suffering in hell, causes a lack of wealth due to the remaining result. Sexual misconduct, when one returns to the human realm after suffering in hell, causes many enemies due to the remaining result. Su-
47:
"One should not kill living beings, one should not take what is not given, one should not commit sexual misconduct, one should not speak falsehoods, one should not drink intoxicants. What is called killing leads to hell, leads to the animal realm, leads to the realm of hungry ghosts. Likewise, stealing and the others also lead to hell, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts. Having been cooked in hell, when one returns to the human realm, as a remaining result of the act of killing, it leads to a short life. Stealing leads to a lack of wealth. Sexual misconduct leads to having many enemies. Falsehood leads to being falsely accused. Drinking intoxicants leads to madness." Thus, he taught these dangers in the five enmities.

The King was by nature faithless, without devotion, and immoral. To an immoral person, talk of virtue is like a spike piercing the ear. Therefore, that King thought, "I came thinking, 'I will support these ascetics.' But from the moment I arrived, they have been attacking and piercing me, speaking in the midst of the assembly. I will do to them what should be done." After the conclusion of the Dhamma talk, he invited them, saying, "Teachers, please accept alms at my house tomorrow," and departed.

On the second day, he had large pots brought and filled with excrement, then had their mouths covered with banana leaves and placed here and there. Furthermore, he had pots filled with slippery resin, honey-oil, and nagabala-mucilage placed at the top of the stairs. At that very spot, he stationed great wrestlers with their loins girded, holding clubs in their hands, and commanded, "These fraudulent ascetics have greatly harassed me. When they descend from the palace, pour the oil at the top of the stairs, strike their heads with clubs, seize them by the neck, and throw them down the stairs." At the foot of the stairs, he had fierce dogs tied up.

The ascetics also exhorted one another, saying, "Tomorrow we shall eat at the King's palace." "Friends, a King's palace is a place of suspicion and danger. Those who have gone forth must be restrained in the six sense doors. One should not grasp at signs in whatever objects are seen. One should establish restraint over the eye-door."
48:
The next morning, at the time for alms-round, they put on their bark garments, placed their black antelope skins over one shoulder, arranged their matted hair well, took their alms bowls, and ascended the King's palace in order. When King Nāḷikira knew that the ascetics had ascended, he had the banana leaves removed from the mouths of the pots filled with excrement. Then, the foul stench struck the nostrils of the ascetics so severely that it was as if their brains were collapsing like falling dry leaves. The Great Ascetic looked at the King. The King said, "O ascetics, eat as much as you desire from these pots, and take some if you wish. This foul filth is suitable for you. Yesterday, I came thinking I would support you, but you only attacked and pierced me, speaking in the midst of the assembly. This liquid filth is very suitable for you; eat it!" and he offered the excrement to the Great Ascetic with a ladle. The Great Ascetic, saying "Shame! Shame!", turned back. "Will you leave with only this much?" the King said, and having the slippery resin poured on the stairs, he gave the signal to the wrestlers. The wrestlers struck the ascetics' heads with clubs, seized them by the neck, and threw them down the stairs. Not a single one could stand on the stairs; they rolled down and reached the foot of the stairs. As each one arrived, the fierce dogs tore them apart and ate them with the sound "paṭa-paṭa". Even those who tried to get up and flee fell into a pit. There too, the dogs pursued and ate them. Thus, the dogs left only the skeletons of those ascetics. In this way, that King deprived the five hundred virtuous ascetics of their lives in a single day.

Afterward, in his kingdom, the deities caused nine types of rain to fall as before. His country was covered by a mound of sand sixty yojanas high. Therefore, the Bodhisatta named Sarabhaṅga said:
"The king who deceives the restrained ones who have gone forth,
Who speak the Dhamma, the blameless recluses,
That Nāḷikera, in the next world, the dogs of hell
Shall gather and devour while he is still trembling."
Thus, it should be understood how the forest of Kāliṅga became a wilderness.

In the past, in the city of Bārāṇasī, there was a daughter of a merchant worth four hundred million named Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, who was beautiful and inspiring. Because she was endowed with beauty, wealth, and noble birth, she was desired by many. Whoever...
49:
Whoever sent a proposal for marriage to Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, upon seeing him, she would find some fault in his lineage or his limbs and the like, saying, 'Who is this low-born, ill-formed person?' and so on. Having him driven away, she would say, 'That I should have seen such a person! Bring water, I will wash my eyes,' and she would wash her eyes. Because she caused every person she saw to be treated with such contempt and driven away, she became known only as 'Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā' (One who finds omens in what is seen), and her original name disappeared.

One day, she planned to play in the waters of the Ganges. She had the landing place prepared, filled carts with many kinds of food, took scents and garlands, and left her house in a covered carriage surrounded by a group of relatives. At that time, the Great Being was born into a Caṇḍāla family and lived in a leather-covered hut outside the city; his name was Mātanga. When he reached the age of sixteen, wishing to enter the city for some business, he dressed in a worn blue cloth, wrapped another around his hand, and holding a basket in one hand and a bell in the other, he rang it to let people know, saying, 'Move aside, masters, I am a Caṇḍāla.' Maintaining a humble mind and paying respect to every person he saw, he entered the city and proceeded along the main road.

Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā heard the sound of the bell and looked through the curtain. Seeing him approaching from afar, she asked, 'Who is this?' 'It is Mātanga the Caṇḍāla, my lady,' they replied. Then Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā said, 'Friends, what evil have we done? Of what karma is this the result? Destruction has surely come upon me! While going on an auspicious errand, I have seen a Caṇḍāla.' Trembling and filled with loathing, she spat and said to her nurses, 'Bring water quickly! I have seen a Caṇḍāla; I will wash my eyes and my mouth that spoke.' After washing, she had the carriage turned back, sent all the prepared provisions home, and ascended her mansion.

The drunkards and her attendants asked, 'Friends, where is Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā? She has not come even at this hour.' Hearing the news, they said, 'Friends, because of this Caṇḍāla, we have lost the chance to enjoy the great feast of liquor, meat, scents, and garlands. Seize the Caṇḍāla!' They searched for where he had gone, and threatening the innocent Mātanga the Wise, they said, 'Hey Mātanga, because of you, we have lost the enjoyment of such gifts!'
50:
(Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā's attendants) seized Mātanga by the hair, threw him to the ground, and beat him with their knees, elbows, stones, and the like. Thinking he was dead, they dragged him by the feet and cast him onto a rubbish heap.

When the Great Being regained consciousness, he felt his limbs and thought, 'On account of whom has this suffering arisen?' Realizing, 'It is not on account of anyone else, but on account of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā,' he thought, 'If I am a true man, I shall make her fall at my feet.' Trembling, he went to the gate of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā's family home and lay down in the courtyard, thinking, 'I will rise only if I get Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā; if I do not get her, I shall die right here.' At that time, this was the custom in Jambudīpa: if a Caṇḍāla, being angry, dies while lying at the entrance of a room, all those living in that room become Caṇḍālas. If he dies in the middle of the house, all the household members; if at the doorway, the residents of the two adjacent houses; if in the courtyard, the residents of fourteen houses—seven on this side and seven on that—all become Caṇḍālas. The Bodhisatta, however, lay in the courtyard.

They informed the merchant, 'Lord Merchant, Mātanga is lying in your courtyard.' The merchant said, 'Go, friends, why is he lying there?' and told them to give him a māsaka and make him get up. They went and said, 'Take this māsaka and get up.' He replied, 'I am not lying here for the sake of a māsaka; I am lying here for Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā.' When asked, 'What fault is there in Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā?' he said, 'Do you not see her fault? Though I am innocent, her people have brought ruin upon me. I will rise only if I get her; if not, I will not rise.'

They went back and informed the merchant. The merchant, knowing his daughter's fault, sent them again, saying, 'Go, give him a kahāpaṇa.' He said, 'I do not want a kahāpaṇa; I want only her.' Hearing this, the merchant and his wife were struck with agitation, thinking, 'We have only this one dear daughter, and there is no other child to continue the lineage.' They said, 'Go, dear friends, if someone among us who is intolerant should take this Caṇḍāla's life, we shall all be ruined if he dies. Guard him!' They arranged for his protection and sent gruel, rice, and wealth, but he rejected everything. In this way, one day passed, then two, three, four, and five days passed.
51:
Then the neighbors living in seven houses each arose and said, "We cannot become Caṇḍālas because of you; do not destroy us. Give your daughter and make this Caṇḍāla get up." Although the merchant and his wife sent a hundred, a thousand, and a hundred thousand in wealth, Mātaṅga continued to refuse. In this way, six days passed. On the seventh day, the residents of the fourteen houses from both sides gathered and said, "We cannot become Caṇḍālas. Even if you do not wish it, we shall give the daughter to this Caṇḍāla."

The parents, as if pierced by the arrow of grief, fell onto their bed in a swoon. The residents of the fourteen houses from both sides ascended the palace and, like breaking a well-bloomed branch of a flame-of-the-forest tree, stripped Diṭṭhamangalikā of all her ornaments. They parted her hair with their nails, cut it short and tied it, dressed her in blue cloth, wrapped blue rags around her hands, adorned her ears with leaden plates, gave her a palm-leaf basket, and brought her down from the palace. Holding her by both arms, they gave her to the Great Being, saying, "Take your husband and go."

The delicate young girl, who had never before carried a burden—to whom even a blue lotus seemed too heavy—said, "Arise, lord, let us go." The Bodhisatta, still lying down, said, "I cannot get up." When she asked, "Then what should I say?", he replied, "Call me, 'Lord Mātaṅga, please arise'." She called him accordingly. He then said, "Your people have made me unable to rise; hold me by the arms and lift me up." She did as he asked. The Bodhisatta, pretending to rise, rolled over and fell to the ground, lamenting, "O friends, Diṭṭhamangalikā has ruined me! First she had me beaten by her people, and now she beats me herself!" When Diṭṭhamangalikā asked, "Lord, what should I do?", he said, "Hold me with both hands and lift me up." She lifted him up and made him sit, then said, "Lord, let us go (gacchāma)." He replied, "'Gaccha' (trees) are only in the forest; we are humans. I have been so severely beaten by your people that I cannot go on foot. Carry me on your back." She bowed her body and offered her back. The Bodhisatta climbed onto her back. When she asked, "Lord, where shall I carry you?", he said, "Carry me out of the city." She went to the East Gate and asked, "Lord, is this your dwelling place?" When he asked, "What place is this?", she replied, "It is the East Gate, lord." He said, "Caṇḍālas are not permitted to live at the East Gate," and without telling her his dwelling place, he made her wander to all the gates. Why?
52:
(He thought,) "I will humble her pride which has reached the highest point of existence (Bhavagga)." The multitude shouted, "Except for one like you, there is no other who can break this woman's pride."

When she reached the West Gate, she asked, "Lord, is this your dwelling place?" When the Bodhisatta asked, "What place is this?", she replied, "Lord, it is the West Gate." He said, "Go out through this gate, look for a leather-covered house, and go there." She went there and asked, "Lord, is this leather house your dwelling place?" He replied, "Yes," and getting off her back, he entered the leather house.

While staying there for seven or eight days, the Wise One seeking Omniscience did not engage in any sexual union during those days. He thought, "If this daughter of a noble family does not attain great status and wealth through me, then I am not a disciple of the twenty-four Buddhas. I shall make the kings of the entire Jambudīpa use this woman's foot-washing water for their consecration ceremonies." Then he thought again, "I cannot achieve this while living in a house; I can only do so by ordaining as a monk." Having thought thus, he addressed her, "Diṭṭhamangalikā, previously when I traveled alone, I could live whether I worked or not. Now, however, I have the responsibility of supporting a wife, and it is impossible to live without working. Wait for me without worrying until I return." He then entered the forest, collected rags from cemeteries and other places, made them into robes, and ordained as an ascetic. Living alone and attaining physical seclusion, he practiced the kasiṇa preliminary exercises and attained the eight meditative attainments and the five superknowledges. Thinking, "Now I am able to be a refuge for Diṭṭhamangalikā," he headed toward Vārāṇasī. Wearing his robes and wandering for alms, he arrived in front of Diṭṭhamangalikā's house.

Seeing him standing at the door, she did not recognize him and said, "Pass on, Bhante, this is a dwelling place of Caṇḍālas." The Bodhisatta remained standing right there. Looking at him again and again, she recognized him, beat her breast with her hands, and crying out, fell at his feet, saying, "Lord, if you had such an intention, why did you cause me to fall from great wealth and leave me helpless?" After lamenting in various ways, she wiped her eyes, arose, took his alms bowl, invited him to sit inside the house, and offered him alms-food. After the Great Being had finished his meal, he said, "Diṭṭhamangalikā, do not grieve, do not lament. I am able to make the kings of the entire Jambudīpa perform their consecration ceremonies with your foot-washing water. You..."
53:
"But follow this one word of mine: enter the city and wander throughout the whole town, proclaiming, 'My husband is not a Caṇḍāla; my husband is the Great Brahmā!'"

When this was said, Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā said, "Lord, I have already come to ruin simply because of the fault of my speech; I cannot speak in such a way." The Bodhisatta said, "How is that? While you lived in my house, did you ever hear any untruthful word from me? Even when I was that man, I did not speak untruths; now that I have become an ascetic, why would I say so? I am known as a man of truth." He then said, "Today is the eighth day of the fortnight. You must proclaim throughout the whole city, 'On the Uposatha day, seven days from now, my husband, the Great Brahmā, will break through the moon's disk and come to me,'" and then he departed.

Believing him, she became very joyful and courageous. She entered the city in the evenings and mornings and made that proclamation. People clapped their hands and laughed in mockery, saying, "Look at this! Our Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā is turning a Caṇḍāla's son into the Great Brahmā."

On the following days, she likewise entered the city in the evenings and mornings and proclaimed, "Now, after six days, five days, four days, three days, two days, and one day, my husband, the Great Brahmā, will break through the moon's disk and come to me."

The Brahmins thought, "This Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā speaks with great courage; perhaps it might be so. Come, let us prepare the place where Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā resides." They leveled the area around the outside of the leather-covered house and scattered sand. On the morning of the Uposatha day, she also entered the city and proclaimed, "Today my husband will arrive."

The Brahmins thought, "Friends, this Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā is not referring to a distant time; she says the Great Brahmā will come this very day. Let us prepare the place." They had the leather-covered house swept, smeared it with fresh cow dung, surrounded it with new unwashed cloths, prepared a throne worthy of noble beings, hung a cloth ceiling above, and suspended garlands of scents and flowers. While they were making these preparations, the sun set.

As the moon rose, the Great Being entered the Jhana which is the basis for higher knowledge. Emerging from it, he performed the preparatory work with sense-sphere wholesome consciousness, and with the consciousness of psychic power, he created a Brahma form twelve yojanas in size. He then flew into the sky and entered the interior of the moon's mansion...
54:
The Great Being approached the moon as it emerged from the forest, and having broken through the moon's mansion and departed from it, he resolved, "Let the great multitude see me," and stood before them. When the people saw him, they said, "Friends, the word of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā is true! Let us worship the arriving Great Brahmā!" Taking scents and flowers, they stood surrounding Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā's house.

The Great Being circled the city of Vārāṇasī seven times from the sky. Knowing that the multitude had seen him, he discarded the twelve-yojana form, created a form the size of a human, and while the multitude was watching, he entered the leather-covered house. When the people saw this, they said, "Our Great Brahmā has descended! Bring a curtain!" and they stood surrounding the house with a large curtain.

The Great Being sat in the middle of the auspicious couch. Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā stood nearby. Then he asked her, "Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, is it your fertile season?" "Yes, Lord," she replied. "Receive the son given by me," he said, and touched her navel with his thumb. By that mere touch, she conceived. The Great Being said, "Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, by this much, your foot-washing water shall become the consecration water for the kings in the whole of Jambudīpa. You remain here." Having said this, he created his Brahma form again, and in the sight of the watching multitude, he departed, flew into the sky, and re-entered the moon's disk.

From that time on, she became known as Brahmapajāpatī. There was no one who could obtain her foot-washing water easily. The Brahmins consulted, "We will have Brahmapajāpatī live inside the city." They placed her on a golden palanquin, and they did not allow those whose lineage was impure for seven generations to hold the palanquin; only sixteen Brahmins of pure birth carried it. The remaining Brahmins worshipped her with scents and flowers and brought her into the city. They consulted, "Friends, it is not proper for Brahmapajāpatī to live in an old house discarded by others. We shall take a plot of land and build a new house. Until it is finished, let her stay in a pavilion."

From then on, those who wished to worship her by merely seeing her with their eyes had to pay one Kahāpaṇa to do so. Those who wished to worship her by hearing her from the vicinity had to pay one hundred. Those who wished to worship her from a place where they could hear her natural speech nearby had to pay five hundred. Those who wished to worship by placing their heads upon her feet had to pay one thousand. Those who desired her foot-washing water obtained it by paying ten thousand. The wealth obtained while she was coming from outside the city to the pavilion inside the city alone amounted to one hundred crores.
55:
The whole of Jambudīpa was shaken. At that time, all the kings, thinking, "We shall perform the consecration with the water used for washing the feet of the Great Brahma's wife (Diṭṭhamangalikā)," sent one hundred thousand each and obtained the foot-washing water. While she was staying in the pavilion, she gave birth. The boy born on account of that Great Being (Mātaṅga Paṇḍita) was pleasing to look at and possessed of auspicious marks. A great uproar spread throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, saying, "A son of the Great Brahma is born!" Wealth amounting to a thousand crores arrived from various places, intended for the boy's milk-money and as birth-gifts. With this wealth, the residence was also completed. Planning to perform the naming ceremony for the boy, they prepared the house, bathed the boy with scented water, adorned him, and because he was born in a pavilion (maṇḍapa), they named him "Maṇḍavya."

As the boy grew up in comfort and reached the age for learning arts and sciences, teachers from all over Jambudīpa came to him to teach those arts. The boy was endowed with wisdom that could penetrate things in an instant and analytical knowledge. He could memorize whatever he heard as if stringing it together. Whatever he learned remained as stable as oil poured into a golden jar. There was no oral tradition of learning that he had not mastered. Brahmins surrounded him as he went about. He also became a constant provider for the Brahmins. Eighty thousand Brahmins ate their daily meals and delicacies at his house. His house was very grand, with seven gatehouses. On the day of the housewarming ceremony, the wealth sent by the inhabitants of Jambudīpa amounted to a thousand crores.

The Bodhisatta reflected, "Is the youth Maṇḍavya heedless or heedful?" Knowing his heedless state, he thought, "He is living only to feed the Brahmins; he does not know the recipient in whom a gift yields great fruit. I shall go and discipline this Maṇḍavya." Then, putting on his robes and taking his alms-bowl, he thought, "The gatehouses are very narrow; it is not possible to enter through the gates." He came through the air and descended into the open space where the eighty thousand Brahmins were eating. The youth Maṇḍavya, while holding a golden ladle and directing the service, saying, "Give soup here, put rice here," saw the Bodhisatta and became as angry as a cobra struck with a stick, and spoke this verse:

"You with a foul smell and a gloomy face, you of base desires, like a dust-demon..."
56:
“From where do you come, you ill-smelling one,
Like a wretched dust-goblin?
With rags from a dustheap wrapped around your neck,
Who are you, fellow, who are unworthy of offerings?”

Then the Great Being, without getting angry and wishing to admonish him, said:

“Famous youth, this food has been prepared by you.
They are chewing, eating, and drinking it.
Know me as one who lives on the gifts of others.
Let the outcaste (me) also receive the alms-food.”

The youth Maṇḍavya, wishing to show that 'this rice is not prepared for people like you,' said:

“This rice of mine is prepared for the Brahmins.
I, who believe in the rewards of the hereafter, have prepared this rice.
Get away from here! Why are you standing here?
You wretch, people like me do not give to the likes of you.”

Then the Bodhisatta, wishing to show that 'a gift should be given to anyone, whether virtuous or not; just as a seed sown in either low or high ground thrives upon the essence of the earth and the essence of water, so there is no such thing as a fruitless gift, yet a gift given to the virtuous yields great fruit like a seed sown in a good field,' spoke this verse:

“Youth, those who desire fruit sow seeds
In fertile fields, whether on high ground or in the hollows.
In the same way, give your gift with such faith;
You may indeed encounter those worthy of offerings.”

Then the youth Maṇḍavya, overcome with anger, said, “Who gave this shaven-headed one permission to enter?” and after threatening the gatekeepers and others—
57:
“I know the fields in this world where I sow the seeds of merit. Those Brahmins who are well-born are the very excellent fields here.” Having spoken this verse, he said, “Beat this wretch with bamboo splints, grab him by the neck, and throw him out past the seven gatehouses.” Then the Great Being said:

“He who reviles a sage is like one who digs a mountain with his nails, or bites iron with his teeth, or presses down a fire with his own body.”

Having said this, he thought, “If this youth Maṇḍavya causes me to be seized by the hands or feet and causes suffering, he will produce much demerit.” Out of compassion for living beings, he rose into the air and descended in the middle of the main street. When the Blessed One attained omniscience, wishing to clarify this matter, he preached this verse:

“Having said this, Mātaṅga, the sage of true effort, departed through the air while the Brahmins watched.”

At that very moment, the chief of the deities guarding the city twisted Maṇḍavya’s neck. His face was turned backward, his eyes rolled around, he vomited saliva from his mouth, and his body became as stiff as if impaled on a spit. The eighty thousand attendant spirits did the same to the eighty thousand Brahmins. They went quickly and informed Diṭṭhamangalikā, the wife of the Brahmin. She came in great haste, and seeing that distorted condition, she spoke this verse:

“The head is twisted to the back, the arms are stretched out uncontrollably, the eyes are white like those of a dead man. Who has done this to my son?”
58:
Then (the attendants) said to Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā:
"An ascetic has come here, unwashed and dirty, like an earth-spirit from the dust. He wore rags from a rubbish heap around his neck. He is the one who has done this to your son." (Ja. 1.15.12)

Upon hearing this, Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā realized: "The noble one who bestowed glory upon me must have come out of compassion, knowing my son's negligence in merit." Then she asked the attendants:
