## The Explanation of the Kīṭāgiri Sutta is finished.
## The Explanation of the Second Division (Vagga) is finished.
136:
## 3. Paribbājaka Vagga
## 1. Commentary on the Tevijjavacchasutta

This discourse beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Tevijjavacchasutta. In that sutta, regarding "ekapuṇḍarīke," the white mango tree is called *puṇḍarīka*. Because there is only one such white mango tree in that grove, it is called *Ekapuṇḍarīka*. "Etadahosi" means that such a thought occurred because of the desire to enter that grove. "Cirassaṃ kho bhante" is said in reference to the fact that [the Buddha] had naturally come there before. In the phrase "dhammassa cānudhammaṃ," omniscience (*sabbaññutañāṇa*) is called "Dhamma," and the teaching of it to the great multitude is called "Anudhamma." The remaining words are exactly as explained in the Jīvakasutta.

"Na me te" means that without consenting to the wanderer's words, [the Buddha] rejects even what should be consented to. For while the statement "The Blessed One is all-knowing, all-seeing, and claims absolute knowledge and vision" should be consented to, the statement "Whether I am walking... [it is always] present" should not be consented to. This is because he knows only after adverting with his omniscience. Therefore, standing on what is not to be consented to, he speaks thus, wishing to reject even what should be consented to.

In the phrase "āsavānaṃ khayā," the word "yāvadeva" is not used because once the taints (*āsavas*) are destroyed, they do not need to be destroyed again. Here, the Blessed One shows the quality of knowing the past through the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*), the quality of knowing the present through the divine eye (*dibbacakkhuñāṇa*), and the supramundane quality through the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhayañāṇa*). Thus, with these three knowledges (*vijjā*), he taught by summarizing all the qualities of a Buddha.

"Gihisaṃyojanaṃ" refers to the lay fetter, which is the craving (*taṇhā*) and attachment to lay requisites. "Natthi kho vaccha" means that there is no one who can make an end of suffering without abandoning the lay fetter. For even though Santati the Minister, Uggasena the merchant's son, and the youth Vītasoka attained Arahantship while in lay form, they did so only after drying up attachment to all formations (*saṅkhāras*) through the Path (*magga*). After reaching Arahantship, however, they did not remain in that form. The lay form is inferior and cannot sustain the supreme quality of Arahantship. Therefore, one who reaches Arahantship in lay form must either go forth [as a monk] or attain Parinibbāna on that very day. Earth-dwelling deities (*bhummadevā*), however, can remain [in their form] because they have places to hide and seclude themselves. In the remaining sense-sphere, among humans, the three types of persons beginning with Stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) can remain.
137:
Stream-enterers and Once-returners reside in the sense-sphere heavens. However, Non-returners and Arahants do not remain there in the form of those deities. Why? Because that place called the sense-sphere heaven is the abode of beings who delight in sensual pleasures, and there is no secluded place suitable for the seclusion of those Non-returners and Arahants. Thus, an Arahant attains Parinibbāna there, and a Non-returner, after passing away, is reborn in the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa). Above the sense-sphere heavens, however, all four types of noble disciples (ariyas) can reside in the form of those Brahmas.

"So pāsi kammavādī" means that the Bodhisatta was also a proponent of action (kammavādī); he did not reject the efficacy of action (kiriyā). This was spoken by [the Buddha] referring to himself ninety-one aeons ago. At that time, it is said the Great Being went forth to examine and take up a sect; even though he knew the fruitlessness of that sect, he did not diminish his effort, and being a proponent of action (kiriyavādī), he was reborn in heaven. Therefore, he spoke thus. The rest of the words are clear in all respects.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## The Explanation of the Tevijjavacchagotta Sutta is finished.
## 2. Explanation of the Aggivacchagotta Sutta

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Aggivacchagotta Sutta. Therein, in the first instance of "na kho ahaṃ" (not I), it means "I am not one with an eternalist view." In the second instance, it means "I am not one with an annihilationist view." Thus, the rejection in all instances should be understood by way of the extremes of finitude and infinitude, etc. This view, "it both is and is not," is partial eternalism (ekaccasassatavāda). This view, "it neither is nor is not," should be understood as eel-wriggling (amarāvikkhepa).

"Sadukkhaṃ" means suffering together with the suffering of defilements (kilesa-dukkha) and the suffering of results (vipāka-dukkha). "Savighātaṃ" means being with distress by way of those two [types of suffering]. "Saupāyāsaṃ" means being with despair by way of those two. "Sapariḷāhaṃ" means being with feverish burning by way of those two.

"Kiñci diṭṭhigataṃ" is a question asking whether there is any single view that has been liked, accepted, and held. "Apanītaṃ" means removed or discarded. "Diṭṭhaṃ" means seen with wisdom. Therefore, it is because he saw the arising and passing away of the five aggregates. "Sabbamanyitānaṃ" refers to all three types of imaginings: imagining through craving (taṇhā-manyita), imagining through views (diṭṭhi-manyita), and imagining through pride (māna-manyita). "Mathitānaṃ" is a synonym for those same imaginings. Now, wishing to show them by analyzing them, he said, "of all I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency of pride" (sabba-ahaṃkāra-mamaṃkāra-mānānusayānaṃ).
138:
In this context, 'ahaṃkāra' (I-making), which is the clinging to 'I', is called 'diṭṭhi' (wrong view). 'Mamaṃkāra' (mine-making), which is the clinging to 'mine', is called 'taṇhā' (craving). 'Mānānusaya' is called 'māna' (conceit). 'Anupādā vimutto' means being liberated without clinging to any of the four types of clinging (upādāna) regarding any phenomena (dhamma).

'Na upeti' means it is not fitting (not logical). In this instance, although the statement 'na upappajjati' (does not reappear) should be permitted, if it were said so, that wanderer (paribbājaka) might adopt the view of annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi). If it were said 'upappajjati' (reappears), he might adopt eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi); if 'upappajjati ca na ca upappajjati', he might adopt partial-eternalism (ekaccasassata-diṭṭhi); and if 'neva upappajjati na na upappajjati', he might adopt the view of equivocation (amarāvikkhepa-diṭṭhi). Therefore, the Blessed One, intending that 'this wanderer should be without a footing and without a support, and should not find an opportunity for easy entry (understanding)', remained without giving permission and even rejected what should have been permitted. 'Alaṃ' means capable or sufficient. 'Dhammo' refers to the law of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). 'Aññatrayogena' means by other efforts. 'Aññatrācariyakena' means by living in the presence of other teachers who do not know the law of dependent origination.

'Then, Vaccha' means 'Since you say you have fallen into great confusion, I will question you again on this matter.' 'Anāhāro nibbuto' means extinguished without a cause (paccaya).

'Yena rūpena' means by whatever form (rūpa) one might designate the Tathāgata (the Buddha), who is called a 'being', as 'one having form'. 'Gambhīro' means profound in terms of qualities. 'Appameyyo' means immeasurable, such that its extent cannot be grasped. 'Duppariyogāḷho' means difficult to fathom or difficult to know. Just as the great ocean is profound, immeasurable, and difficult to know, so too is the Arahant (khīṇāsava). All statements such as 'reappears' and so on made in reference to that Arahant are illogical. How? Just as all statements such as 'gone to the eastern direction' and so on made in reference to an extinguished fire are not fitting, so it is here.

'Aniccatā' means because of impermanence. 'Sāre patiṭṭhitaṃ' means established in the essence of the supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma). All the remaining words are clear in all places.

## In the Pappañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Aggivacchasutta is finished.
139:
## 3. Commentary on the Mahāvacchasutta

The sutta beginning with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' is the Mahāvacchasutta. In that sutta, 'sahakathī' means one who has conversed with. By saying, 'I have previously had many conversations with the Venerable One,' he recalls past conversations and establishes a friendly rapport. This is because the two previous suttas were also preached to this very wanderer. In the Saṃyutta Nikāya, the section called the Abyākata Saṃyutta was also preached to this wanderer. In the Ekuttara Nikāya (Aṅguttara Nikāya), there are also conversations held with this wanderer, such as 'Master Gotama, is the world eternal? Is only this true and the other futile?' and 'This is an undeclared (abyākata) issue.' Therefore, the wanderer Vaccha said 'sahakathī'. The Blessed One also showed favor and gave an opportunity to that wanderer who came repeatedly. Why did He give the opportunity? Because this wanderer held the view of eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi). Those with the view of eternalism do not quickly abandon their views. Like an old cloth (pilosika) smeared with animal fat and sesame oil, they can only be purified after a long time. The Blessed One saw: 'As time goes by, this wanderer will abandon his view, go forth (ordain) in my presence, realize the six direct knowledges (cha-abhiññā), and become a distinguished disciple.' Therefore, He showed favor and gave an opportunity to that wanderer whenever he arrived. This was the wanderer's final visit. In this sutta, he came with the firm resolve: 'Whether I can cross (the round of rebirths) or not, I will go to the ascetic Gotama and ordain, like one who descends into the water leaning on a staff.' Therefore, wishing to request a Dhamma teaching, he said, 'It would be good if the Venerable Gotama would [teach] me...' and so on. The Blessed One taught Vaccha a brief discourse by way of the roots (mūla) and a detailed discourse by way of the courses of action (kammapatha).

In this sutta, the teaching given by way of the roots is extremely brief, while the teaching given by way of the courses of action, though brief, is like a detailed one. In truth, for the Buddhas, there is no such thing as a detailed teaching in an absolute sense (nippariyāyena). Even the twenty-four books of the Paṭṭhāna and all seven books of the Abhidhamma Piṭaka are merely brief. Therefore, it should be understood that He taught only a summary, both by way of the roots and by way of the courses of action.

In that teaching on the courses of action, the seven factors in sequence beginning with 'abstaining from taking life is wholesome' (pāṇātipātā veramaṇī kusalaṃ) are only of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). However, the three factors beginning with non-covetousness (anabhijjhā) are applicable to all four planes (bhūmi).

In the phrase 'Vaccha, when for a bhikkhu...', although it is stated without specification (as to which bhikkhu), it should be understood that the Blessed One spoke this referring to Himself, just as in the Jīvaka Sutta and the Caṅkī Sutta.
140:
Regarding the question "Atthi pana" (Is there...?), why does he ask? His view is: "In various dispensations, only the teacher is an Arahant; the disciple is unable to reach Arahantship. The ascetic Gotama speaks as if referring to a single monk, saying 'Vacchā, for a monk...'. Is there any disciple of the ascetic Gotama who has reached Arahantship?" He asks with the intention of inquiring about this matter. In that question, "Tiṭṭhatu" means let the Venerable Gotama wait for a moment (meaning it is already known that the Venerable Gotama is a renowned Arahant in the world). When the Buddha answered thus, he further asked questions regarding bhikkhunīs and so forth, and the Blessed One answered him as well.

"Ārādhako" means one who accomplishes or fulfills the practice.

"Sekhāya vijjāya pattabbaṃ" means what should be attained through the three lower fruits. He says, "I have attained all that." A Vitaṇḍavādī (sophist), however, says: "Which states are trainee states (sekha)? According to the words 'The four paths and the three lower fruits of recluseship,' he has reached the path of Arahantship but not yet the fruit. He wants the Buddha to speak about the further exertion to reach that fruit." That Vitaṇḍavādī should be informed thus:

"He who has abandoned five defilements,
Is a fully perfected trainee (sekha) of non-declining nature,
Has attained mastery over the mind and has composed faculties—
Such a man is truly called one of steady nature."

An Anāgāmī (Non-returner) is indeed a fully perfected trainee. Referring to him, it was said: "What should be attained through the knowledge of a trainee." Since the path (magga) lasts only for a single thought-moment, there can be no questioning of one standing in that path. If it is said that according to this sutta, the path also has many thought-moments, that is not the word of the Buddha and contradicts the meaning of the quoted verse. Therefore, it should be understood that while standing in the fruit of Non-returning, he is made to speak about the insight (vipassanā) for the path of Arahantship. Because he had the potential (upanissaya) not only for pure Arahantship but also for the six higher knowledges (abhiññā), the Blessed One, thinking, "In this way, by working on tranquility (samatha), he will produce the five higher knowledges; by working on insight (vipassanā), he will reach Arahantship; thus he will become a great disciple with six higher knowledges (chaḷabhiñño mahāsāvako)," did not teach insight alone but taught both tranquility and insight.
141:
"Sati satiāyataneti" means mindfulness in the cause of mindfulness. What is the cause here? It should be understood that the cause is either higher knowledge (abhiññā), or the meditative absorption (jhāna) which is the basis for higher knowledge, or ultimately, fruition of Arahantship (arahattaphala), or insight (vipassanā) which is the cause of Arahantship.

"The Blessed One has been served by me" means that the seven types of trainees (sekha) are said to be currently serving the Blessed One, but only the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava/arahant) has completed the service to the Blessed One. Thus, the Elder Mahāvaccha spoke in this way, declaring his attainment of Arahantship in brief. Those monks, not understanding that meaning, accepted the Elder's words and reported them to the Blessed One. "Devatā" refers to a deity who possesses those qualities. All the remaining words are clear in meaning in every instance.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## The Explanation of the Mahāvacchasutta is finished.
## 4. The Explanation of the Dīghanakhasutta

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Dīghanakhasutta. In that sutta, "Sūkarakhatāyaṃ" means in the cave named Sūkarakhatā. It is heard that during the time of Kassapa Buddha, that cave became buried underground as the earth rose during the interval between two Buddhas. Then, one day, a pig dug the earth near the edge of the cave's roof. When it rained, the earth was washed away, and the edge of the roof became visible. A forest hunter saw it and thought, "This cave must have been used by virtuous ones in the past; I will renovate it." He removed the surrounding earth, cleaned the cave, built walls, and installed doors and windows. Having completed the plasterwork and painting, he spread sand that looked like silver plates, arranged couches and stools, and offered it for the Blessed One to reside in. The cave was deep, so one had to descend and ascend to use it. This was said in reference to that fact.

"Dīghanakha" is the name of that wanderer (paribbājaka). Why did he approach? It is heard that when the Elder Sāriputta had been ordained for half a month, Dīghanakha thought: "My uncle does not stay long when he goes to other sects. But now, it has been half a month since he went to the ascetic Gotama. I have not heard any news of him..."
142:
"Is the teaching potent? I shall find out," with such a desire to go, he (Dīghanakha) arose. Therefore, he approached (the Blessed One). "Standing to one side" means that at that time, the Elder Sāriputta was standing fanning the Blessed One. Dīghanakha the wanderer, out of shame and fear towards his maternal uncle (the Elder), asked the question while standing. Referring to that, it is said, "standing to one side."

"Everything is not pleasing to me" means "All rebirths (upapatti) are not pleasing to me; taking conception (paṭisandhi) is not pleasing to me." By saying this much, he indicates, "I am an annihilationist." The Blessed One, setting aside his (annihilationist) intention for a moment, wishing to show the fault in the phrasing "Everything is not pleasing to me" first, spoke the words beginning with "Even this [view] of yours." Therein, "Is even this view of yours not pleasing?" means "Is even this view, which you first liked, accepted, and held, not pleasing (to you)?"

"Master Gotama, if this view were pleasing to me" means "I have the view 'Everything is not pleasing to me'; to me who is such, this view 'Everything is not pleasing to me' would be pleasing." The statement "Everything is not pleasing to me" is just like that for him. Just as this view is pleasing even though it is included in the general grasp of "everything," so too would that view be pleasing. Thus, seeing the fault placed upon his own doctrine, he speaks with the intention, "I shall resolve that fault." However, in meaning, it follows for him that "This view is not pleasing to me." If this view is not pleasing or liked by someone, then for him, through that view, the view "Everything is not pleasing to me" is liked. If that is so, by not liking or not being pleased with the view, it follows that "He likes everything." But he does not admit that meaning; he merely holds onto the cessation (of life) through his annihilationist view.

Therefore, the Blessed One said, "Aggivessana, than those (who abandon) ... they cling to another view." Therein, "ato" is the ablative case (nissakka) used in comparison with those who abandon. It means that those who do not abandon (their views) are far more numerous than those who do. In "bahū hi bahutara," the word "hi" is a mere particle, and it means "are far more numerous." Later, in the phrase "tanū hi tanutara," the same method applies. "Those who spoke thus" means "those who say so." "They do not abandon that view and cling to another view" means they do not give up the original view but cling to another view.

Here also, having taken the eternalist view, it is not possible to take the annihilationist view or the partial-eternalist view without abandoning that (original) view. Having taken the annihilationist view, it is not possible to take the eternalist view or the partial-eternalist view without abandoning that view. Having taken the partial-eternalist view, it is not possible to take the eternalist view or the annihilationist view without abandoning that view. But the original eternalist view...
143:
Without abandoning the original eternalist view, it is possible to take only another eternalist view. How? At one time, having taken "Form is eternal," at another time one takes "Not only pure form is eternal, but feeling is also eternal, consciousness is also eternal." The same method applies to the annihilationist view and the partial-eternalist view. As it is applied to the aggregates, so should it be applied to the sense bases. Referring to this kind of grasping, it is said, "They do not abandon that view and cling to another view."

In the second instance, "ato" means "than those who do not abandon" (ablative case). Those who abandon are far fewer than those who do not abandon. "They abandon that view and do not take another view" means they abandon that original view and do not take any other view. How? At one time, having taken "Form is eternal," at another time, seeing the danger in that view, one abandons it, thinking, "This view of mine is gross." One relinquishes it, reflecting, "Not only is the view 'Form is eternal' gross, but the view 'Feeling is eternal ... consciousness is eternal' is also gross." The same method applies to the annihilationist view and the partial-eternalist view. As with the aggregates, so should it be applied to the sense bases. In this way, they abandon that original view and do not take another view.

Why did He undertake this teaching beginning with "Santa, Aggivessana"? This Dīghanakha the wanderer, who held an annihilationist view, was hiding his own view. Thinking that if the merits of that view were spoken, he would reveal his own view, the Blessed One undertook this teaching to show and analyze the three views together.

In the phrases beginning with "sārāgāya santike," it means being near to being attached to the round of rebirths by the power of lust, and being near to being fettered to the round by the fetters of craving and views. "Abhinandanāya" means being near to swallowing and grasping by the power of craving and views. In the phrases beginning with "asārāgāya santike," the meaning should be understood as being near to not being attached to the round, and so forth.

Among these views, the eternalist view is less blameworthy but hard to relinquish. The annihilationist view is more blameworthy but can be relinquished quickly. How? An eternalist knows that this world and the next world exist. He knows that there are results of good and bad deeds. He performs wholesome deeds and is afraid to perform unwholesome deeds. He enjoys and delights in the round of rebirths.
144:
A person with the eternalist view, even when coming face to face with the Buddhas or the disciples of the Buddha, is unable to quickly abandon their own view. Therefore, that eternalist view is said to be of little fault but slow to be dispelled. On the other hand, an annihilationist knows that this world and the next world exist, and knows that there are fruits of good and bad deeds; however, they do not perform wholesome deeds, do not fear when performing unwholesome deeds, do not delight in the cycle of rebirth, and without being greatly attached, they are able to quickly abandon their view when face to face with the Buddhas or the disciples of the Buddha. If they are able to fulfill the perfections, they become a Buddha and attain Parinibbāna; if unable to fulfill them, they make a resolution, become a disciple, and attain Parinibbāna. Therefore, the annihilationist view is said to be of great fault but can be quickly dispelled.

That wanderer Dīghanakha, without being able to note the meaning thus explained, thought, "The Buddha praises my view; my view is certainly very good," and spoke the words beginning with "Ukkāṃseti me bhavaṃ."

Now, this wanderer is filled only with the annihilationist view, like a bitter gourd filled with sour gruel. Just as it is impossible to put oil, molasses, etc., into a gourd without discarding the sour gruel, and even if put in, it cannot be received, similarly, without abandoning that view, one is not worthy of attaining the Path and Fruit. Therefore, to cause the abandoning of the view, the Blessed One exerted effort with the words beginning with "Tatragghivessana." "Viggaha" means dispute. "Thus there is the abandoning of those views" means that by seeing the faults such as dispute, those views are abandoned. That wanderer, reflecting "What benefit is there for me in this dispute and so forth?", abandoned that annihilationist view.

Then the Blessed One, intending to fill the heart of Dīghanakha with the deathless medicine, like putting ghee, molasses, etc., into a gourd from which the sour gruel has been vomited out, and wishing to show insight (Vipassanā), spoke the words beginning with "Ayaṃ kho pana Aggivessana kāyo." The meaning of those words has been explained in the Vammika Sutta. The words beginning with "Aniccato" have also been detailed below. "Yo kāyasmiṃ kāyachando" means the craving that arises in the body. "Sneho" is the very moisture of craving. "Kāyanvayatā" means the state of following the body, meaning the defilements that follow the body.

Having thus shown the meditation subject of materiality (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna), now wishing to show the meditation subject of immateriality (arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna), He spoke the words beginning with "Tisso kho." Again, wishing to show the unmixed nature of those feelings, He spoke the words beginning with "Yasmiṃ Aggivessana samaye." In that text...
145:
The summary of the meaning is: At the time when one feels one of the feelings such as pleasant feeling, at that time, the feelings other than the one being felt are not "sitting" waiting for their turn or opportunity. In fact, those feelings have not yet arisen, or they have vanished like bursting water bubbles. The words beginning with "Sukhāpi kho" were spoken to show the manner of the total disintegration of those feelings.

"Na kenaci saṃvadati" means that by holding the eternalist view and saying "I am an eternalist," one does not dispute with an annihilationist; and by holding that same eternalist view and saying "I am an eternalist," one does not dispute with a partial-eternalist. In this way, the three views should be applied interchangeably. "Yañca loke" refers to the speech used and spoken in the world; without misinterpreting or clinging to any phenomenon, one speaks according to worldly usage. It has also been taught thus:

"The monk who is an Arahant, who has finished his task,
Whose outflows are exhausted, and who bears his final body,
He might say, 'I speak,'
And he might say, 'They speak to me.'
Being skilled in the designations used in the world, and understanding them,
He would speak merely by way of worldly usage." (from Saṃyutta Nikāya).

In another text, it is taught: "Citta, these are worldly designations, worldly expressions, worldly usages, worldly concepts, which the Tathāgata uses without clinging." (from Dīgha Nikāya).

"Abhiññāpahānamāha" means that in regard to eternalism and so forth, having known those various phenomena as eternal with higher knowledge, He taught the abandoning of the eternalist view; having known annihilationism and partial-eternalism with higher knowledge, He spoke of their abandoning. Having known form with higher knowledge, He spoke of the abandoning of form—in this manner, the meaning should be understood here.

"Paṭisañcikkhato" means for one who reflects. "Anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimucci" means the mind was liberated from defilements without clinging to the outflows which are ceased through the cessation of non-arising. By this much, just as one dispels hunger by eating rice cooked for another, the Venerable Sāriputta, by sending his knowledge into the teaching given for another, the wanderer Dīghanakha, and developing insight, reached the Fruit of Arahantship. He stood having reached the pinnacle of the disciple's perfection of knowledge and having penetrated the sixteen types of intellectual speed (javana). The wanderer Dīghanakha also reached the Fruit of Stream-entry and was established in the Three Refuges. The Blessed One, having concluded this teaching, descended from Gijjhakūṭa Hill, went to the Veḷuvana Monastery, and held an assembly of the disciples.
146:
Venerable Sāriputta, directing his knowledge to the Dhamma teaching given for another (the wanderer Dīghanakha) and developing insight, attained the fruit of Arahantship. He stood having penetrated the peak of the knowledge of a disciple's perfection and the sixteen types of knowledge. The wanderer Dīghanakha, however, attained the fruit of Stream-entry and became established in the refuges.

The Blessed One, having concluded this teaching while the sun was still up (before sunset), descended from Gijjhakūṭa Mountain, went to Veḷuvana Monastery, and held an assembly of disciples. That assembly was endowed with four factors. These factors are: it was the full-moon Uposatha day associated with the Māgha constellation; one thousand two hundred and fifty monks assembled of their own accord without being invited by anyone; among those monks, there was not a single worldling, nor anyone among the Stream-enterers, Once-returners, Non-returners, or dry-insight Arahants, but all were Arahants with the six higher powers; and among those monks, there was not a single one ordained by cutting the hair with a razor, but all were 'Ehi-bhikkhu' monks.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## The Explanation of the Dīghanakha Sutta is finished.
## 5. Explanation of the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta. Therein, "aggāgāre" means in a fire-offering hall. Regarding the term "tiṇasanthārake"—there were two people named Māgaṇḍiya, an uncle and a nephew. Between them, the uncle had ordained and attained the fruit of Arahantship. The nephew also possessed the supporting conditions (upanissaya) and would soon ordain and attain the fruit of Arahantship. Then, the Blessed One, seeing his supporting conditions, left the delightful Gandhakuṭi chamber, which is like a divine chamber, and stayed for a few days in that fire-offering hall, which was soiled with ashes, grass, and rubbish, having a grass mat spread out for the sake of helping another. It was with reference to that stay that this was said. "Tenupasaṅkami" means he did not approach only on that day. The reason is that the fire-offering hall was located near the village and was crowded and not secluded due to boys and girls. Therefore, the Blessed One would always spend the daytime in that forest grove and go to that fire-offering hall in the evening to stay.
147:
The Blessed One, while usually putting away the grass mat and making a mark before leaving on other days, left it spread out on that day. Why? Because, having surveyed the world at dawn that day, he saw: "Today, Māgaṇḍiya will come here, see this grass mat, and start a conversation with Bhāradvāja concerning the grass mat. Then I will come and teach the Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma, he will ordain in my presence and attain the fruit of Arahantship. Indeed, I have fulfilled the perfections only for the sake of helping and supporting others." Thus, he left having spread out the grass mat.

"I think this grass mat is a place suitable for a recluse." This place is not the dwelling of an unrestrained recluse. For in this place, no marks of being pulled by the hand, pulled by the foot, or struck by the head are apparent; it is like a mat spread out by a skilled artist who has marked it with a brush, without disorder, without confusion, and without being broken. This is the dwelling place of a restrained recluse. He asked, "Friend, whose dwelling place is this?"

"It is the place of the Bhūnahu (the destroyer of growth, the maker of boundaries)," he said. Why did he say so? Because he [the Buddha] was perceived as having the doctrine of the cessation of growth in the six doors. For this was his [Māgaṇḍiya's] doctrine: "The eye should be increased, should be developed; the unseen visible form should be seen; the seen visible form should be surpassed. The ear should be increased, should be developed; the unheard sound should be heard; the heard sound should be surpassed. The nose should be increased, should be developed; the unsmelled odor should be smelled; the smelled odor should be surpassed. The tongue should be increased, should be developed; the untasted flavor should be tasted; the tasted flavor should be surpassed. The body should be increased, should be developed; the untouched tangible should be touched; the touched tangible should be surpassed. The mind should be increased, should be developed; the unknown mental object should be known; the known mental object should be surpassed." Thus, he prescribes growth in the six doors.

The Blessed One, however, taught:
"Restraint of the eye is good, good is restraint of the ear.
Restraint of the nose is good, good is restraint of the tongue.
Restraint of the body is good, good is restraint of speech.
Restraint of the mind is good, good is restraint in everything.
The monk restrained in everything is freed from all suffering."
(Dhp. 360-361)
148:
(The Blessed One) prescribes restraint in the six sense-doors. Therefore, that Māgandiya, thinking "The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer of growth, a maker of restrictions," said "Bhūnahu (destroyer of growth/embryo)."

"Ariye ñāye dhamme kusale" refers to the pure and blameless causal Dhamma. What is shown by this? One who is to speak about such a famous, well-known, and influential person should speak after investigating and reflecting, keeping a guard over the mouth. Therefore, it shows: "Do not speak hastily; keep a guard over the mouth." In saying "It comes thus in our scripture," it means: "Because it comes thus in our scripture, we do not speak merely what comes to the mouth as we wish; what should those who speak what is found in the scripture fear? Therefore, we can say it even to his face." "Appossukka" means being unconcerned and without effort for the sake of protecting me. "Vutto va naṃ vadeyya" means: "Being exactly as I, Māgandiya, have spoken, and without being asked (by Master Gotama), starting the conversation and filling it in as if taking mangoes, rose-apples, etc., may Master Bharadvāja speak in the manner I have spoken; please speak."

"Assosi kho" means the Blessed One, having developed the light-kasina, saw Māgandiya who had arrived there with his divine eye. He also heard the sound of the two people talking with his divine ear. "Paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito" refers to the time when he emerged from the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti). "Saṃvigga" means being shaken and agitated with joyful emotion (pīti-saṃvega). To that Brahmin Bharadvāja, this thought occurred: "Māgandiya has not yet informed the ascetic Gotama, nor have I. Apart from the two of us, there is no third person; that person with sharp hearing must have heard our voices." Then, joy arose within him, and ninety-nine thousand hairs stood on end. Therefore, it is said: "Saṃvigga lomahaṭṭhajāta (agitated, with hair standing on end)." "Atha kho māgandiyo paribbājako" means that for the wanderer Māgandiya, his wisdom reached maturity like a seed with an opening face. Therefore, unable to remain seated, he wandered about and returned once more to the Blessed One and sat at a respectful distance. To show that sitting, it is said "Atha kho māgandiyo," and so on.

The Blessed One did not say, "Māgandiya, you said this about me," but instead began the Dhamma teaching to the wanderer Māgandiya with "Cakkhuṃ kho māgandiya..."
149:
In the sense of being the dwelling place of eye-consciousness, the visible form is the delight of the eye; therefore, the eye is called 'rūpārāma.' Because it delights in forms, it is 'rūparata.' Because forms greatly gladden eye-consciousness, it is 'rūpasamudita.' 'Danta' means tamed or not indulged in. 'Gutta' means secured. 'Rakkhita' means guarded. 'Saṃvuta' means closed off. 'Saṃvarāya' means for the purpose of restraint. 'Paricāritapubba' means formerly much enjoyed. 'Rūpapariḷāha' is the fever of defilements arising with visible forms as the object. The Blessed One asked, "Māgandiya, what would you say to this Arahant who, having comprehended visible forms with insight-wisdom, has reached the fruit of Arahantship? Would you say 'He is a destroyer of growth, a maker of restrictions,' or not?" Māgandiya replied, "Master Gotama, there is nothing at all to be said." In the case of the remaining sense-doors, it is the same way. Now, just as you, Māgandiya, have nothing to say to an Arahant who has reached the fruit of Arahantship by comprehending the five aggregates with insight-wisdom, so too have I reached omniscience by comprehending the five aggregates; therefore, to show "You should not say anything to me," He said "Ahaṃ kho pana," and so on. "Tassa mayhaṃ māgandiya" was said to show his own luxury during his life as Prince Siddhartha when he was a layman. Among those terms, "Vassika" refers to the palace comfortable for living in during the rainy season. In the remaining terms, it is the same way. Here, the word-definition is: living for the four months of the rains is "vassa"; because it is suitable for living in the rains, it is "vassika." In the remaining terms, it is the same way. 

Among those palaces, the Vassika palace used during the rainy season is neither too high nor too low. The main doors and air-windows of that palace are neither too thin nor too many. In this palace, only floor coverings, bedspreads, and food and snacks that are balanced in heat and cold are suitable. In the Hemantika palace used during the winter, the pillars and walls are low. The main doors and air-windows are thin with subtle openings. Wall-projections are removed to allow heat to enter. In this palace, floor coverings, bedspreads, and clothing such as blankets that have the power to provide heat are suitable. As for food and snacks, those containing ghee and butter with a pungent taste are suitable. In the Gimhika palace used during the summer, the pillars and walls are high. In this palace, the main doors and air-windows are numerous with large lattices. Floor coverings and so on made of dukūla silk are suitable. Food and snacks that have a sweet taste and cooling properties are suitable. In this palace, new pots filled with water are placed near the air-windows and covered with blue lotuses and so on. In various places...
150:
Just as streams of water appear when the rain-god pours down rain, water machines were made through which streams of water emerged.

Furthermore, for the Bodhisatta, one hundred and eight golden pots and one hundred and eight silver pots were filled with scented water, and after arranging clusters of blue lotuses in them, they were placed surrounding the bed. In large copper cauldrons, scented mud was filled, and blue lotuses, red lotuses, and white lotuses were planted; these were placed here and there to capture the coolness. The lotus flowers bloomed by the rays of the sun. Various groups of bees entered the palace and flew about, taking nectar from the flowers. The palace was filled with an exceedingly fragrant scent. Between the double walls, copper pipes were installed, and in the open air above the nine-story palace, a net with fine holes was fastened over a jeweled pavilion. In one place, a dried buffalo hide was spread out. When the Bodhisatta played in the water, they threw stone balls onto the buffalo hide; that sound was like the thundering of clouds. Below, they turned the machine; the water rose up and fell from above the net, appearing like falling raindrops. At that time, the Bodhisatta wore blue garments, covered himself with a blue robe, and adorned himself with blue ornaments. His retinue of forty thousand female dancers also wore blue clothes and ornaments and were anointed with blue unguents; surrounding the Great Being (Mahāpurisa), they went to the jeweled pavilion. During the day, while playing in the water, he enjoyed the comfort of the cool season.

In the four directions of the palace, there were four ponds. During the day, groups of birds of various colors would rise from the eastern pond and, chirping, fly over the palace to the western pond. Rising from the western pond, they would fly to the eastern pond; from the northern pond to the southern pond; and from the southern pond to the northern pond. (Their constant flying) was like the rainy season. The palace for the winter season had five stories, and the palace for the rainy season had seven stories.

'Nippurisehi' means devoid of men (consisting only of women). In this context, it was not only the musical instruments that were without men; all places were without men. The doorkeepers were only women, and those who performed services such as bathing were also only women. It is said that the King thought: "If a person enjoying such sovereign happiness and prosperity sees a man, doubt may arise; that doubt of mine..."
151:
"Let no (doubt) arise in my son," thinking thus, the King placed only women in all affairs. The phrase "delighting in that delight" was said with reference to the delight in the attainment of the fruit (phalasamāpatti) based on the fourth jhāna.

In the phrase "a householder or a householder's son," the meaning should be understood thus: because for nobles (khattiyas), there is only the aspiration for the white parasol (sovereignty), and their impediments (papañca) are many; and brahmins, never satisfied with the Vedas, wander about seeking the Vedas; but householders, from the time they learn the art of finger-counting (arithmetic), only enjoy prosperity. Therefore, without including nobles and brahmins, he said, "a householder or a householder's son." "Āvaṭṭeyya" means that one might return because of the cause of human sensual pleasures. "Abhikkantatarā" means more excellent. "Paṇītatarā" means more refined (or more difficult to be satisfied with). This was also said:

"If one were to take water from the ocean with the tip of a blade of kusa grass and compare it with the water in the ocean, even so, human sensual pleasures are very few in the presence of divine sensual pleasures."

"Samadhigayha tiṭṭhati" means that having attained divine happiness, one stands far surpassing that divine prosperity.

In this context, the comparison between the simile and the thing signified (opammasansandana) should be understood thus: the time when the householder is endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure is like the time when the Bodhisatta, Prince Siddhattha, delighted among forty thousand women in the three palaces. The time when that householder, having fulfilled good conduct, is reborn in heaven is like the time when the Bodhisatta renounced the world and realized omniscience upon the throne of enlightenment (bodhipallaṅka). The time when that householder enjoys prosperity in the Nandana Grove is like the time when the Tathāgata passes time in the delight of the attainment of the fruit of the fourth jhāna. The time when that householder does not long for the five cords of human sensual pleasure is like the time when the Tathāgata, while passing time with the attainment of the fruit of the fourth jhāna, does not long for the happiness of inferior people.

"Sukhī" means one who, though having reached suffering first, later reaches happiness. "Serī" means one who, though living with a physician first, later becomes independent and alone. "Sayamvasī" means one who, at first, had to follow the will of a physician, sitting when told to sit, lying down when told to lie down, eating when told to eat, and drinking when told to drink, but later becomes self-controlled. Which...
152:
The ability to go wherever one wishes means that although at first one is unable to go to a desired place, later, when the illness has subsided, one can go wherever one wishes, such as to see forests, hills, or mountains. Wherever one desires to go, there one can indeed go.

In this comparison, the correlation between the simile and the thing signified is as follows: The time when the man was afflicted with leprosy is like the time when the Bodhisatta lived in the household. A single pit of glowing coals is like a single object of sensual pleasure. Two pits of glowing coals are like two objects. The two and a half crores of pits of glowing coals belonging to Sakka, the king of devas, are like the two and a half crores of dancers. Scratching the openings of the wounds with fingernails and heating them over a pit of glowing coals is like indulging in objects of sensual pleasure. The time of being free from illness through medicine is like the time when the Bodhisatta, having seen the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefits in renunciation, went forth and became a Buddha, spending his time in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) based on the fourth jhāna. The time of not envying another person afflicted with leprosy is like the time when the Buddha, spending his time in that bliss, does not desire the pleasure of low people.

"One with impaired senses" refers to one whose physical sensitivity (kāyaprasāda) is destroyed by worm-leprosy. "Those with impaired senses" refers to those with an impaired wisdom faculty (paññindriya). Just as that leper with impaired physical sensitivity perceives the painful touch of fire as pleasant through a perverted perception, so too, because of the impairment of the wisdom faculty, they perceive sensual pleasures, which are of painful touch, as pleasant through a perverted perception.

Regarding the words "asucitarāni ceva" and so on: By nature, those wounds are impure, foul-smelling, and putrid. Now (during scratching and heating), they become even more impure, even more foul-smelling, and even more putrid. When that person heats the wounds and scratches the itch, small worms enter inside, and corrupt blood and pus flow out. In this way, there is only a mere measure of gratification for him.

In the verse beginning with "ārogayaparamā": Among whatever gains of wealth, gains of followers, or gains of children there may be, health is the highest and most excellent; there is no gain superior to it. Therefore, "health is the highest gain." Among whatever bliss of jhāna, bliss of the path, or bliss of fruition there may be, Nibbāna is the highest; there is no bliss superior to it. Therefore, "Nibbāna is the highest bliss." The Eightfold Path, which occurs in the preliminary stage of the supramundane path and leads to the Deathless, is secure; there is no other secure path superior to it. Alternatively, in the text "khemaṃ amatagāminī," both the names "khemaṃ" and "amataṃ" are names for Nibbāna. Those other doctrines of recluses and brahmins, which are held by the power of their own views as leading to the place of security and leading to the Deathless...
153:
In the verse beginning with "Ārogyaparamā," the meaning should be understood as follows: In the world, there are various types of gains, such as gaining wealth, gaining followers, and gaining children. Among these gains, being free from illness is the most excellent. There is no gain superior to being free from illness. Therefore, it is said, "Ārogyaparamā lābhā" (Health is the highest gain). There are all kinds of bliss, such as the bliss of jhāna, the bliss of the Path, and the bliss of the Fruition. Among these, the bliss of Nibbāna is the most excellent. There is no bliss superior to the bliss of Nibbāna. Therefore, it is said, "Nibbānaṃ paramaṃ sukhaṃ" (Nibbāna is the supreme bliss).

"Aṭṭhaṅgiko maggānaṃ" means that the Eightfold Path, which is the way to Nibbāna through practice in the preliminary stage of the Supramundane Path, is the secure way. There is no other secure path superior to this path. Alternatively, in the phrase "khemaṃ amatagāminī," both the names "khema" (security) and "amata" (deathless) are names for Nibbāna itself. There are other doctrines of recluses and brahmins who, according to their own views, hold that their paths lead to security and the Deathless. Among all those paths (views) claimed to lead to the security of Nibbāna, the Noble Eightfold Path is the most supreme and excellent; this is the meaning here.

"Ācariyapācariyānaṃ" means of the teachers and of the teachers' teachers (the lineage). "Sameti" means it is similar or identical, without distinction, like measuring with a single measure or weighing with a single scale. "Anomajjati" means stroking repeatedly by lowering the hand. "Venerable Gotama, this is health, this is Nibbāna," he says, stroking sometimes the head and sometimes the chest.

"Chekaṃ" means accomplished or skilled. "Sāhuḷicīrena" refers to taking a coarse cloth made of black sheep's wool. Some also call it "saṅkāracola" (rags collected from a dust heap). "Vācaṃ nicchāreyya" means he should speak while repeatedly stroking sometimes at the beginning, sometimes at the edge, and sometimes in the middle. "Pubbakehesā" should be analyzed as "pubbakehi esā." Indeed, the Blessed One Vipassī... and the Blessed One Kassapa, while seated in the midst of the fourfold assembly, spoke this verse. The great multitude learned it as "a verse based on welfare" (atthanissitagāthā). After the Parinibbāna of the Buddha, it entered among the wanderers (paribbājakas). Although those wanderers put it into books, they were only able to preserve the two lines: "Ārogyaparamā lābhā, nibbānaṃ paramaṃ sukhaṃ." Therefore, He said, "That verse has now gradually become a verse of worldlings (puthujjanagāthā)."

"Rogova bhūto" means "rogabhūta" because the disease itself has become manifest. The same method applies to the remaining terms. "Ariyaṃ cakkhu" refers to pure insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) and path knowledge (magga-ñāṇa). "Pahoti" means being capable. "Bhesajjaṃ kareyya" means one should perform medical treatment such as emetics, purgatives, and eye drops.

"Na cakkhူni uppādeyya" means that if someone's visual sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) is impaired due to being enveloped by bile, phlegm, etc., they can produce eyes (gain sight) by relying on a skilled physician and using suitable medicine. However, for one born blind (jaccandha), the sensitivities were already destroyed even in the mother's womb. Therefore, such a person cannot obtain sight. Thus, He said, "He would not produce eyes." In the second instance, "jaccandha" refers to one who is blind from birth due to being enveloped by bile and so on. "Amitto" means that one should look upon the person who gave the coarse cloth made of black sheep's wool mentioned earlier as an enemy, thinking, "This person is my enemy." The same should be understood for the second term, "paccatthikato." "Anumiyamānaṃ" refers to that which is known by the mind that follows along in the beginningless Saṃsāra. With the words "tassa me upādānapaccayā," He taught the Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) which has one connection and two layers, and clearly showed the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa). "Dhammānudhammapaṭipanno" refers to the practice that is in accordance with the Dhamma of Nibbāna and is the means of escape from the cycle. With the words "this disease, ailment, dart," He showed the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhā). With the words "upādānanirodhā," He showed the cessation. The Buddha spoke thus, wishing to teach in this way. The remaining expressions in all places have the same meaning as previously stated.

## End of the Commentary on Māgaṇḍiya Sutta.
## The fifth, Māgaṇḍiya Sutta, is finished.
